Meta adds that personalized features can help deliver age-appropriate experiences.

The business model

There is also a commercial interest at stake: engagement. How often people return, how long they stay, and how much they interact all matter to the platforms’ businesses.

Meta’s annual report says it generates substantially all its revenue from advertising. It also says that changes to its content displays and product features can affect time spent, user engagement, and financial results. That doesn’t establish why the companies sued, but it helps explain why restrictions on recommendations and autoplay could have financial consequences.

If removing these features leads people to spend less time on a service, it could mean fewer opportunities to show ads. Compliance would also require product and operational changes, such as checking users’ ages and providing a different experience to those under 16.

Youth is the future. Big Tech is very much aware of this. Meta’s annual report identifies youth as an investment priority and describes attracting and retaining users as a competitive objective. Restrictions affecting how young people join and use a platform could affect its longer-term audience strategy, too.

What the future will bring

California is challenging an important part of the attention-based business model. Meta’s annual report warns investors that regulation affecting how it displays content or serves younger users could affect user growth, engagement, and financial results.

And then there’s the matter of age verification. The required age checks could affect adults as well as children: a service must verify users’ ages before providing the restricted features. Depending on how the checks work, this could involve sharing age-related information, raising privacy concerns and creating another opportunity for sensitive data to be exposed in a breach.

If it were up to me, platforms would stop designing for compulsive use, whatever the user’s age. Adults deserve a healthier online experience too. Applying those protections to everyone would also remove the need to check someone’s age before deciding whether they can use these features. Platforms might lose some advertising opportunities, but time spent online should not be the only measure of a successful service.

Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once.

items.title: New Dark Project Ransomware Group Offers Hackers 80% Commission to Expand Cyberattacks
items.summary: A ransomware group called Dark Project is recruiting criminal partners with an offer of 80% of proceeds from successful attacks, pairing generous commissions with a platform for managing extortion. First observed in June 2026, the financially motivated operation combines data theft, file encryption, and public leak threats to pressure organizations into paying. The group’s published victim records cover 38 organizations across eight countries, with the United States accounting for 30 listings. Manufacturing, healthcare, and construction feature prominently. However, these figures describe organizations named in threat intelligence and leak-site records, not independently verified compromises or a complete measure of the group’s activity. Researchers from Gurucul identified Dark Project’s ransomware operation in their threat actor profile, documenting its recruitment process, infrastructure, and reported attack methods. Their findings describe an emerging operation that uses the language of legitimate security services to advertise tools and partner support for ransomware activity. New Dark Project Ransomware Group Dark Project advertises a partner program under which affiliates receive 80% of proceeds while its operators retain 20% for platform services and reporting. The offer resembles established ransomware affiliate revenue models used by other criminal groups, although the advertised terms do not prove that partners receive payments as promised. Recruitment follows four stages: application, vetting and onboarding, deployment, and commission settlement. Applicants contact the group through Tox. Approved partners reportedly receive a unique identifier, platform access, and operational instructions before deploying payloads against organizations. Dark Project claims to manage victim communication and ransom negotiations, promising commission payments within 24 hours of a completed engagement. The advertised infrastructure includes a Tor-hosted operations dashboard, agents supplied in EXE and BIN formats, and a social-engineering simulation suite. Agents reportedly contain partner identifiers that allow activity to be linked to individual affiliates. These are platform claims documented by Gurucul, rather than capabilities independently demonstrated through published malware analysis. Bitcoin Payment Instructions and Cryptocurrency Settlement Process (Source – Gurucul) Separating payload deployment from negotiations gives affiliates fewer operational tasks to manage. Comparable affiliate management platform features have appeared in Lynx ransomware operations, where partners can manage victim profiles and leak schedules. Dark Project also promotes Bitcoin payments, but the supplied report provides no wallet addresses or transaction evidence confirming settlements. Victim disclosures peaked in August 2026, when 20 organizations were listed, following four in June and none in July. September and October each added five listings, while November contributed four at collection time. These dates track publication activity; they should not be treated as confirmed intrusion dates. Reported Attack Methods, Defensive Priorities, and Evidence Gaps Gurucul describes initial access through phishing, exposed Remote Desktop Protocol services, compromised credentials, and VPN access sourced from infostealer logs or initial access brokers. The reported operation targets Windows environments and follows double-extortion, stealing sensitive information before encryption and threatening publication if negotiations fail. This creates separate risks involving business disruption and data exposure. That distinction matters because restoring files does not remove the threat of stolen information becoming public. Related reporting on data theft extortion tactics explains why recovery alone cannot resolve every ransom demand. Dark Project’s Tor leak site serves as its public pressure channel, publishing alleged victim details when the operators seek additional leverage. The report maps activity to techniques including abuse of valid accounts, Windows Management Instrumentation, RDP, SMB, data exfiltration, encryption, and attempts to inhibit recovery. It also lists associated vulnerabilities, but does not provide sufficient incident evidence to establish every listed flaw as a confirmed Dark Project entry point. Defenders should distinguish reported associations from demonstrated exploitation. Manufacturing accounts for 12 reported victims, healthcare for seven, and construction for four. Those concentrations make access monitoring and recovery readiness important priorities for exposed organizations. Gurucul recommends patching, stronger access controls, suspicious-activity monitoring, and secure backups. Security teams can use those measures without assuming that every affiliate follows an identical intrusion sequence. items.title: Pinpointing Location of Videos from Background Airplane Sounds
items.summary: This is fascinating : The video describes a technique that can reveal where an otherwise unidentifiable recording was made by analyzing its audio for the faint sounds of passing aircraft. The technique is both fascinating and frightening. It works by looking at Doppler curves, which plot the way a plane’s sound changes as it passes overhead because of the Doppler effect. This is the same familiar Doppler effect that causes the frequency of a siren to rise as it approaches and then fall as it passes by and moves away. More generally, it’s the phenomenon whereby the frequency of a wave perceived by an observer changes when the observer and the source of the wave are moving in relation to one another. […] It’s sound that’s relevant here, though, and specifically the sound of aeroplanes. Early in his video, Colsto brings up a map of the flights that were in the air at the time the video he’s tracing was recorded. Much of this information is publicly available. Aircraft equipped with Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) transmit data about their position, velocity, and altitude, which flight-tracking services collect and make available to the public. While not every plane is tracked, the system provides an enormous amount of information about aircraft movements.

items.title: Microsoft Warns Fake Game Downloads Are Secretly Monetizing Windows PCs
items.summary: Fake game downloads and cracked software installers are turning Windows PCs into money-making tools for campaign operators. Microsoft has warned that deceptive installation packages quietly deliver software that shares internet bandwidth, runs distributed-computing workloads, or installs unwanted utilities, often without users understanding what they have agreed to install. The campaign targets people searching for free games, software activators, audio plugins, and unofficial tools. Unlike the password theft seen in fake game download campaigns , this operation focuses on making money from installed software and device resources. A single installer can attempt several installations, giving operators multiple opportunities to profit from one download. Microsoft Threat Intelligence researchers identified the campaign and detailed its behavior in a November 3 technical report. Their investigation confirmed three delivery branches involving WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine and BOINC, and Advanced Windows Manager. These products can have legitimate uses; the security concern is their installation through deceptive bundles without informed consent. Microsoft Warns Fake Game Downloads The infection starts when someone runs an installer presented as a game, cracked application, or utility. Observed lures included PC games, Roblox executors, auto-clickers, and driver tools. The package launches temporary processes built around Inno Setup, then starts additional executable stages that deliver the bundled software. Not every installation follows an identical sequence. The delivery system calls its downstream packages “offers” and tracks their results separately. Session, affiliate, and offer values help coordinate delivery and record outcomes. Importantly, one failed offer does not mean the entire bundle has stopped: another package can still install successfully. Some payloads also launched before or around their reporting callback, making those reports incomplete prevention checkpoints. Attack chain (Source – Microsoft) WorldProxyPool supplies the bandwidth-sharing branch, routing third-party internet traffic through affected devices. The underlying risk resembles proxyware disguised as Notepad++ , where apparently useful downloads conceal unauthorized network sharing. In Microsoft’s investigation, scheduled tasks launched the proxy agent at startup, ran a hidden PowerShell watchdog every five minutes, and checked for updates hourly, all with SYSTEM privileges. The computing branch installs CharityEngine, BOINC, and supporting components, including VirtualBox. Microsoft observed computing workloads, hardware-capability checks, and communication with CharityEngine infrastructure. This is resource hijacking, but the findings do not establish cryptocurrency mining. The distinction matters because distributed computing and cryptomining are different activities, even when either consumes resources without the owner’s informed permission. A third branch installs Advanced Windows Manager or Windows Manager utilities and updater components. Across the campaign, unattended installation options reduce visible prompts. The result is not necessarily one obvious malicious program, but a collection of unexpected applications and recurring background activity that can outlast the original download session. Detection, Protection, and Campaign Indicators Microsoft recommends avoiding cracked software, unofficial game installers, and activation tools, while enabling cloud-delivered protection, tamper protection, and reputation-based controls. Its unwanted software protection guidance also explains why potentially unwanted applications deserve attention even when they are not classified as malware. For organizations, software inventory reviews can reveal installations that users never intended to authorize. Utility download lure (Source – Microsoft) Investigators should connect suspicious installer execution with network callbacks, newly created scheduled tasks, and unexpected software. Earlier YouTube download proxyware campaigns demonstrate how ordinary download activity can conceal persistent bandwidth sharing. However, that reporting concerns separate activity; Microsoft’s report does not establish a connection between those operators and this campaign. items.title: Anthropic’s Claude Code Reportedly Leaks User Email Addresses Through HTTP User-Agent Headers
items.summary: Anthropic’s Claude Code is facing privacy concerns after a user reported that the AI coding tool sent their email address to third-party websites through HTTP User-Agent headers during web searches, without permission. The report raises questions about how coding agents handle personal data while carrying out routine tasks. GitHub user taylor-edwards filed issue #107757 on November 5, 2026, saying they now receive “dozens of scam emails per day.” Their setup included Claude Code version 2.1.318 on macOS, running inside tmux. The user demanded that the behavior be removed entirely rather than controlled through a setting. The issue does not include a raw HTTP request, a sample header, or steps to reproduce the behavior. While other users reported similar experiences, the public evidence does not establish that the alleged exposure caused the scam emails or affected every Claude Code user. Claude Code Leaks User Email A User-Agent header normally identifies the software making a web request. An email placed inside that header reaches the destination website alongside the request. This makes the issue a potential privacy leak through routine web access, rather than a reported theft of Anthropic’s account database. The discussion points to model-written commands as a possible route. A quoted explanation in the thread describes Claude using an email available in its context as a contact address when writing a curl request. This differs from the malicious traffic routing covered in unauthorized Claude Code relay services , where third parties changed client settings. In the GitHub issue , poteat said versions 2.1.317 and later include a built-in module called cc-plugin-privacy , designed to block this behavior. The contributor said it is enabled by default and can be disabled through /plugins . However, the original reporter was already using the newer 2.1.318 release. Several commenters questioned whether the protection worked as intended. Some could not find the module, while others said harmless local tests containing their account email and User-Agent text ran without being blocked. Those tests did not transmit personal data, but they raised questions about whether the guard was active and effective. A separate comment quoted a Claude Code employee saying Anthropic planned to remove account emails from model context in an upcoming release. That statement also acknowledged gaps in the interim protection. The issue remained open when reviewed. Teams should review agent-written network commands and verify privacy controls before allowing web access. Earlier reporting on Claude Code security-rule bypasses highlights a related lesson: a configured safeguard should not be treated as proof that sensitive data cannot leave a system. items.title: Hackers Launch 240,000 Exploit Attempts WordPress Core Flaw Enabling Remote Code Execution
items.summary: Hackers have launched more than 240,000 exploit attempts against a WordPress Core vulnerability that can allow attackers to run malicious code without logging in. According to the supplied Wordfence report, attacks began on October 28, 2026, the same day WordPress released a security update addressing the flaw. Tracked as CVE-2026-119977 , the vulnerability carries a high severity CVSS score of 8.1. It affects unpatched WordPress branches from 4.7 through 7.1.3. Researcher Umut Bayram reported the weakness, which involves predictable, publicly accessible folders created during full WordPress Core upgrades. WordPress addressed the issue in its October 28 security release, alongside several other security fixes. Older branches also received backported patches. Cybersecuritynews.com’s earlier coverage of WordPress 7.1.4 security fixes explained how the update changes temporary folder handling to reduce exposure during upgrades. 240,000 WordPress Exploit Attempts During a full upgrade, WordPress extracts installation files into a temporary folder beneath /wp-content/upgrade/ . On vulnerable installations, predictable folder names can let attackers find this separate installer through a web request while the update remains in progress. No existing WordPress account or user interaction is required. The attack depends on a race condition, meaning the attacker must reach those files at the right moment. The temporary installer must remain accessible long enough to complete the attack before cleanup removes it. This timing requirement makes successful exploitation difficult, even when attackers repeatedly probe known paths. The official WordPress release announcement confirms that the upgrade weakness can lead to remote code execution. The CVE record classifies it as a time-of-check, time-of-use race condition, with high potential impact on data confidentiality, integrity, and availability. According to the supplied Wordfence analysis, attackers reaching the exposed installer could complete a staged installation, create an administrator account, and upload malicious PHP code. That access could support backdoors, content changes, or data theft. Observed requests targeted installer files inside predictable upgrade directories. Wordfence’s supplied figures show attack traffic peaked on October 30, when its firewall blocked more than 74,000 requests. Activity was highest between October 29 and November 1. These figures describe blocked requests, not confirmed infections, successful code execution, or the number of individual websites affected. Earlier reporting on 60,000 WordPress attack attempts made the same distinction. Repeated automated requests can increase the chance of finding an exposed installer, but request totals alone cannot establish whether attackers completed the required steps or gained lasting access. Administrators should install WordPress 7.1.4 or the corresponding patched release for their branch. Automatic background updates may have installed the fix, but owners should verify completion. WordPress recommends immediate updating and notes that only its latest release receives active support. Updating from a vulnerable version still uses its existing upgrade process once. The supplied Wordfence guidance recommends blocking public access to PHP files beneath /wp-content/upgrade/ before updating. Its protection requires Extended Protection mode because staged PHP files run outside normal WordPress loading. items.summary_html:
Hackers have launched more than 240,000 exploit attempts against a WordPress Core vulnerability that can allow attackers to run malicious code without logging in. According to the supplied Wordfence report, attacks began on October 28, 2026, the same day WordPress released a security update addressing the flaw.

Tracked as CVE-2026-119977, the vulnerability carries a high severity CVSS score of 8.1. It affects unpatched WordPress branches from 4.7 through 7.1.3. Researcher Umut Bayram reported the weakness, which involves predictable, publicly accessible folders created during full WordPress Core upgrades.

WordPress addressed the issue in its October 28 security release, alongside several other security fixes. Older branches also received backported patches. Cybersecuritynews.com’s earlier coverage of WordPress 7.1.4 security fixes explained how the update changes temporary folder handling to reduce exposure during upgrades.

240,000 WordPress Exploit Attempts

During a full upgrade, WordPress extracts installation files into a temporary folder beneath /wp-content/upgrade/. On vulnerable installations, predictable folder names can let attackers find this separate installer through a web request while the update remains in progress. No existing WordPress account or user interaction is required.

The attack depends on a race condition, meaning the attacker must reach those files at the right moment. The temporary installer must remain accessible long enough to complete the attack before cleanup removes it. This timing requirement makes successful exploitation difficult, even when attackers repeatedly probe known paths.

The official WordPress release announcement confirms that the upgrade weakness can lead to remote code execution. The CVE record classifies it as a time-of-check, time-of-use race condition, with high potential impact on data confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

According to the supplied Wordfence analysis, attackers reaching the exposed installer could complete a staged installation, create an administrator account, and upload malicious PHP code. That access could support backdoors, content changes, or data theft. Observed requests targeted installer files inside predictable upgrade directories.

Wordfence’s supplied figures show attack traffic peaked on October 30, when its firewall blocked more than 74,000 requests. Activity was highest between October 29 and November 1. These figures describe blocked requests, not confirmed infections, successful code execution, or the number of individual websites affected.

Earlier reporting on 60,000 WordPress attack attempts made the same distinction. Repeated automated requests can increase the chance of finding an exposed installer, but request totals alone cannot establish whether attackers completed the required steps or gained lasting access.

Administrators should install WordPress 7.1.4 or the corresponding patched release for their branch. Automatic background updates may have installed the fix, but owners should verify completion. WordPress recommends immediate updating and notes that only its latest release receives active support.

Updating from a vulnerable version still uses its existing upgrade process once. The supplied Wordfence guidance recommends blocking public access to PHP files beneath /wp-content/upgrade/ before updating. Its protection requires Extended Protection mode because staged PHP files run outside normal WordPress loading.

items.title: Mirax Android RAT Hijacks Phones Through Streaming-App Ads to Steal Banking Credentials and Drain Accounts
items.summary: An Android banking malware campaign is turning streaming-app advertisements into a route for stealing credentials and draining accounts. Mirax, the remote access trojan lets criminals watch infected phones, intercept security codes, and operate banking apps directly from victims’ devices. Thousands of Android phones belonging to retail banking customers across the Middle East, Turkey, and Africa were infected between March and September 2026. Confirmed cases point to losses reaching millions of US dollars, although the available figures cover only infections and fraud visible to investigators and affected banks. Group-IB researchers identified the campaign in a November 5 investigation, reporting activity spikes during Eid and late July. The operation remained active when the report was published, with streaming apps assessed as possible advertising vectors still available on Google Play. Mirax Android RAT Hijacks Phones Through Streaming-App Ads Evidence suggests the infection begins inside low-reputation streaming apps downloaded from Google Play. Advertisements and video links direct users toward a separate installer downloaded outside the store. This differs from Perseus streaming app attacks , which use fake IPTV applications distributed through sideloading, but both exploit demand for entertainment. One confirmed installer posed as “TikTok 18+,” an imitation unrelated to TikTok or ByteDance. It retrieves the Mirax payload, which impersonates Google Play Services using a Cyrillic letter that resembles the Latin “o.” The disguise makes a dangerous permission request appear connected to a familiar system component. Accessibility access is the turning point. Mirax pushes victims toward enabling this permission, then uses it to read screen content and control the interface. Banking overlay (Source – Group-IB) Similar Android banking overlay attacks combine permission abuse with counterfeit login screens, helping attackers capture credentials while users believe they are interacting with legitimate applications. Mirax also intercepts SMS messages and notifications, records typed information, and captures lock-screen PINs, passwords, or patterns. Operators can replay those secrets to unlock phones unattended, open banking sessions, add beneficiaries, and initiate transfers. Since transactions originate from the customer’s genuine phone and banking app, familiar device signals provide less reassurance. Researchers found evidence of international transfers, internal account movements, and marketplace purchases. Some proceeds may have passed through mule accounts in India, but investigators were still tracing destinations. The findings do not establish that every transfer followed the same laundering route. Server-Controlled Features Complicate Detection and Response Mirax separates its installed capabilities from its targeting instructions. Banking overlays and application mappings arrive from command-and-control infrastructure after installation rather than being packaged inside the Android application. The observed operation targeted more than 20 banking and wallet packages, alongside global cryptocurrency exchanges. Two WebSocket channels separate commands from stolen data, while HTTP long-polling provides a fallback. Operators can remotely change hosts, ports, TLS settings, and polling intervals. DNS-over-HTTPS is enabled by default, reducing visibility through local DNS monitoring. Static inspection therefore cannot reveal every target or configuration deployed against a particular victim. A SOCKS5 module also turns compromised phones into residential proxies. Earlier reporting on Mirax residential proxy capabilities described how this routes malicious traffic through victims’ connections. ‘Google Play Services’ Interface prompts displayed to targets leading to Accessibility Service authorization (Source – Group-IB) Combined with device takeover, it can weaken checks based on IP reputation and location, without requiring attackers to operate from their own infrastructure. The malware hides its launcher icon, randomizes package names, and restores activity after reboots. It can obstruct uninstall screens, block security applications, and display black overlays or fake updating messages while fraudulent activity continues underneath. These controls extend the time operators have to exploit an infection. Group-IB recommends checking Accessibility abuse, remote-control activity, and screen sharing alongside transaction attempts. Banks should escalate suspicious combinations and hold payments for customer verification. Users should reject unexpected Accessibility requests from entertainment apps, avoid advertised APK downloads, and seek removal support when a suspicious app resists uninstallation. Indicators remain useful, but rotating identifiers make behavioral detection essential. items.title: Integrate Aquasec and Jenkins to Stop Unsafe Images Before They Run
items.summary: TL;DR Attackers now turn a new vulnerability into a working exploit faster than most teams can rebuild and redeploy an image. That makes the build pipeline the last place to stop a known problem, but a pipeline check on its own ends at the push. The Aquasec plugin for Jenkins scans container images inside Pipeline &mldr

items.title: The post-quantum future of web privacy
items.summary: The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS. Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens , which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy. With 10 years of deployment experience under our belts — using Privacy Pass for applications such as privacy proxies (like iCloud Private Relay) and relays (like Privacy Gateway) — we, along with others , are collaborating to bring the next generation of this technology to the web. One of our goals is to develop more sophisticated tools for managing agentic traffic that would otherwise consume too many resources and degrade performance for human visitors. Another goal is to foster a more open ecosystem by making it easier for more types of clients to participate. Achieving these goals requires developing new capabilities beyond what Privacy Pass offers today. Given the trajectory, in this post we look at the prospects for post-quantum. In fact, we're in better shape than one might think. Privacy Pass still relies on classical cryptography, like RSA and elliptic curves. This means that a quantum attacker will be able to forge tokens at will and use them to bypass whatever security mechanism the site operator wants to implement (such as rate limiting). On the other hand, Privacy Pass is unconditionally private, meaning no attacker, quantum or not, can link the redemption of a token to its issuance. What's more, the new capabilities we're developing for this new generation of private authentication technology can and will be instantiated in a way that upholds the same guarantee: your interaction remains private even after Q-day. This gives us a little breathing room, but we will need an alternative soon. This is an active area of research that has made significant strides in recent years. Still, just as is the case with other aspects of the transition, the primary challenge is the sheer size of post-quantum alternatives: ML-DSA-44 signatures are a whopping 2,420 bytes, while ECDSA-P256 signatures are just 64 bytes. And there's not much hope for drop-in replacements any time soon. Just as for TLS, we'll have to settle for primitives with higher cost and re-engineer our systems to bear this cost . But what will those primitives be? In this post, we'll explore one potential future for post-quantum privacy on the web, made possible by a recent breakthrough in the design of blind signatures. What we need to build: a brief look at MOLE Let's start with an overview of this new technology, which is presently called MOLE ("Moderation Of unLinkable Endorsements"). We'll have much more to say about MOLE later on, but for now we'll highlight the details that are most relevant to cryptography. One of the core components of Privacy Pass is a blind signature scheme, which allows a client to obtain a signature under an issuer's secret key without revealing to the issuer the message that it signed. The client can then reveal the message and blind signature later on without linking the signature to its issuance. One type of Privacy Pass token consists of the message and blindly issued signature. To verify the token, the verifier needs the issuer's public key, and so necessarily learns the identity of the issuer. Thus while these tokens protect the identity of the client, they don't protect the identity of the issuer. Of course, this is exactly what we want for some use cases. The identity of the issuer tells us something about what type of client is connecting to our edge, a signal we use to make decisions in some of our products and for some of our customers. For instance, a client might use a token issued by one of our customers to prove it is authorized to use the customer's VPN product. However, for many use cases, this is more information than we actually need to make a decision to grant a client access to a resource. Normally we only care that the token was issued by some entity we trust. In fact, MOLE takes this a step further: the token should hide the identity of the issuer altogether so that we can't treat tokens differently based on who issued them. This guarantees equal treatment regardless of the type of client, making it easier for more clients to participate. This issuer-hiding property is achieved through a new object called an endorsement . An endorsement is issued by an anchor and redeemed by a moderator . Before redemption, the client and moderator agree on an anchor set , the public keys of the anchors trusted by the moderator. During redemption, the client proves it was issued an endorsement by one of the anchors in the anchor set without revealing which one. Upon acceptance, the moderator issues the client the MOLE credential it will use to moderate the client's interaction with the site. An endorsement can take many forms, but its key property is that it can be redeemed while hiding the identity of the anchor that issued it. There will also be many types of credentials, but because they're intended to be used by a particular moderator, they needn't be anchor-hiding or even publicly verifiable. This means that everything from blind signatures to anonymous credit tokens or anonymous rate-limited credentials can be used to instantiate MOLE credentials. Now that we have a sense of what we're building, let's look at our options for post quantum. A feast of cryptography When designing cryptographic protocols, adaptability and efficiency are often in tension. Sometimes we know exactly what we want to build and can tailor a construction for that purpose; but the more we tailor the protocol for that use case, the harder it becomes to adapt that construction to a different use case. Adaptability is essential for a system like MOLE. We're not just building one kind of credential system, but many. And the types of credentials we need are likely to change over time, especially on the web where we must constantly adapt to new traffic patterns and attacker behavior. To keep up, we need a set of building blocks that can be composed together into different protocols to meet different requirements. Most of the post-quantum cryptographic schemes in wide use today come from larger families of constructions, but have been tuned for their particular application. ML-DSA is a good example here: the cryptographic framework from which this scheme was derived can be used to build a variety of things, but to make ML-DSA as compact as possible, its parameters have been carefully tailored to build an efficient and secure digital signature scheme. However, the same parameters would not necessarily be secure for other use cases. We have come to view this as the central challenge for post-quantum anonymous credentials: to decouple parameter selection from protocol design . Classical credential systems take this for granted: for the most part, protocol designers don't need to think about the parameters of the elliptic curve they're using, allowing even non-experts in the design of elliptic curve cryptography to build useful things with it. Unfortunately, designing efficient post-quantum credentials still requires an enormous amount of expertise . This situation seems to have changed, however. Earlier this year, we saw a breakthrough that represents a potential sea change for anonymous credentials. VOLE-in-the-Head The roots of this breakthrough go back several years. We'll pick up the story three years ago, with the VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) zero-knowledge proof system ( Baum et al., Crypto 2023 ). A zero-knowledge proof system allows one to prove knowledge of a hidden witness, satisfying some public statement while keeping the witness private. For example, a zero-knowledge proof can be used to prove knowledge of an AES key K for which Y=AES(K,X) , where X,Y are public. This proof can be transformed into a digital signature whose security reduces to the security of AES, with X,Y as the public key and K as the secret key. This is exactly the FAEST digital signature, a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature competition . Compared to many contemporary proof systems, VOLEitH is relatively simple to understand and implement securely. VOLE stands for "Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation" and is an interactive technique that gives two parties correlated random values. These correlations act like authentication tags, allowing the verifier to check that a computation on the hidden witness was performed correctly. In VOLEitH, the prover prepares locally what the two parties would normally generate together — hence “in the head” — then commits to those values and uses the Fiat-Shamir transformation (a widely used tool in cryptography) to select the parts the verifier checks. This step turns the interactive VOLE process into a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof. Apart from its simplicity, VOLEitH is a fairly unremarkable proof system. It's not succinct in the way many other proof systems are: its proofs are asymptotically linear in the size of the witness and the arithmetic complexity of the statement being proved. However, VOLEitH is concretely very efficient for a particular type of statement, namely one that can be expressed as a set of equations over small binary fields. One example is the relation Y=AES(K,X) we just discussed. We don't normally think of AES as a set of equations, but many of its computations are designed around arithmetic in GF(2 8 ), a field whose elements are single bytes. FAEST proofs for this statement are only about 4KB (NIST Round 3, 128s). Another example is the KuMQuat signature scheme, in which the signer proves an instance of the Multivariate Quadratic (MQ) problem. Here we're given a system of random, quadratic equations of multiple variables over a small field, like GF(2 8 ). Mathematically, this MQ map P looks something like P(s) = (s T A 1 s + b 1 s,…,s T A m s + b m s) where s and each b i are length n vectors and each A i is an n-by-n matrix. Given P,P(s) for random s, the MQ problem is to find s. We call it quadratic because we multiply the elements of s by itself. The MQ problem is believed to be hard to solve even for a quantum computer. But because P is made up of quadratic equations, proving knowledge of a solution with VOLEitH is fairly cheap, yielding KuMQuat signatures as small as 2.6KB. When compared to other post-quantum signatures like ML-DSA or FN-DSA, these numbers don't look especially impressive. But how VOLEitH compares to other schemes in a particular category of constructions is beside the point. For MOLE, we'll need to strike a balance between performance and the ability to build many types of credential systems. To that end, we need one more ingredient. Multivariate signatures Another way to build signatures from MQ maps involves embedding some additional mathematical structure into the map. In the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) signature scheme, the public key is an MQ map P , and a signature is a vector s satisfying P(s) = t , where t is obtained by hashing and salting the message to be signed. The secret key for this signature scheme is a trapdoor for P with which the signer can derive solutions to the MQ equations. The trapdoor reveals to the signer a hidden partitioning of the variables of each quadratic equation into “oil” and “vinegar” variables. Oil variables are never multiplied by one another, so fixing the vinegar values turns the equations into a linear system that the signer can solve for the oil values. In the public key, oil and vinegar variables are mixed together in a way that hides this structure in the map. UOV is also a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature standardization effort. It has one of the smallest signatures among the candidates, at just 135 bytes. The trade-off is that it has the largest public keys, at 46.6KB. MAYO is another multivariate candidate with much smaller public keys, at the cost of slightly larger signatures. The key thing to take away here is that the arithmetic complexity of evaluating a UOV (or MAYO) signature is comparable to evaluating an MQ instance. Both are public quadratic maps over small binary fields, making them a good fit for VOLEitH. This brings us to the breakthrough. Blind signatures from VOLE-in-the-Head and UOV Earlier this year, a blind signature called PoMFRIT was published ( Baum et al., USENIX Security 2026 ) that achieved what at the time was a record for candidate post-quantum constructions: 6.7KB for the blind signature itself and just a few hundred bytes for issuance. PoMFRIT is based on VOLE-in-the-Head and the MAYO multivariate signature. We can easily drive the size of the signature down to 4.3KB by swapping MAYO out for UOV. (This figure uses NIST round 3 parameters for UOV (uov-Ip) and FAEST-EM-128s.) The trade-off is larger public keys, but this pays off in applications where a public key can be cached and used sufficiently often. This is competitive with state-of-the-art lattice-based constructions . But the really good news is that building blocks of PoMFRIT can easily be reconfigured into all of the credential systems we've considered for MOLE, including endorsements. More on this in a bit: for now, let's look at how PoMFRIT works in more detail. A well-known paradigm for designing blind signatures is the following. First, the client places the message in the cryptographic equivalent of a sealed envelope, called a commitment . For our purposes, a commitment is simply the hash of the message together with some randomness generated by the client. To complete issuance, the signer simply signs the commitment directly. To construct the blind signature, the client produces a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of the signature and the randomness it used to compute the commitment, called the opening. A verifier would use the signer's public key to verify this proof. Let's define a bit of notation to make this clearer: The client generates an opening r and sends a commitment c=H(m,r) to its message m to the issuer. The issuer produces a signature s=Sign(sk,c) and sends it to the client. It doesn’t learn the message as it’s hidden behind the hash. Finally, the client produces a proof π of knowledge of s,r for which Verify(pk,H(m,r))=1 , The proof π is the blind signature. It can be verified by any party in possession of the issuer's public key pk and the message m . Unlinkability comes from the client presenting entirely different objects during the two phases: a commitment is shown to the issuer during issuance, and a zero-knowledge proof is shown to a verifier during presentation. Even if the issuer and verifier collude or are the same entity, they cannot link the sessions. The size of the proof π is dominated by evaluation of the hash, so we need to choose a hash function that is friendly for our proof system. For most proof systems, such proof-friendly hashes are not well studied, but for VOLEitH it turns out that the Keccak permutation used in SHAKE and TurboSHAKE is a good choice. Keccak’s bitwise operations translate natively into VOLEitH constraints: XOR becomes addition, AND becomes multiplication, and rotations simply rearrange values. (Many popular SNARKs, by contrast, are designed for large prime fields, making byte- and bit-oriented operations less natural to express.) Nevertheless, Keccak evaluations end up being the largest component of the VOLEitH proof, so we need to make sure we're using only the minimum necessary number of permutations. PoMFRIT requires two: one for the commitment and another for the signature. Concretely, the statement we prove is roughly P(s)=H(H(m,r),r s ) where s is the signature, r s is a salt chosen by the issuer, P is the issuer's UOV public key, and H denotes the Keccak permutation with the output truncated to the appropriate length, which also prevents anyone from inverting. From blind signatures to endorsements and beyond Recall that for MOLE endorsements, we need something like a blind signature, but one that doesn't reveal the anchor that issued it. That is, we now have a sequence of anchor keys P 1 ,…,P N , and the statement we now want to prove is P i (s)=H(H(m,r),r s ) for some anchor key P i whose index i is now part of the hidden witness. With some care, we can write this as a set of constraints with roughly the same cost: two hashes and one MQ evaluation. We need to prove a bit more about the witness. What exactly? We won't spoil it for you: ZK circuit design is part of the craft of cryptographic engineering that makes it so fun. We'll just say the kind of thinking needed here is transferable to just about any modern proof system you might encounter. Even more advanced credential systems can be constructed in this framework, including the aforementioned anonymous credit tokens and anonymous rate-limited credentials. In both of these cases, the primary cost is an additional hash or two. Each of these also requires proving that part of the witness (e.g., the credit count) is in some expected range, but this is low cost in VOLEitH. Indeed, for every construction we have considered so far for MOLE, the primary cost is the size of the Keccak evaluation and how many times we need to evaluate it. This means that finding ways to reduce the amount of hashing yields improvements across the board. Optimizations Before we go any further, we need to acknowledge that cryptanalysis of multivariate cryptography is still relatively immature. We have seen advances against several parameter regimes in just the last couple of years, Both UOV and MAYO have weathered these attacks well, and an outright break of UOV and even MAYO seems more unlikely with every passing year. But we should at least expect the parameters to change in a way that adds a bit of cost to our constructions. On the other hand, it's not uncommon for credential systems used in practice to adopt a less-than-conservative security posture for the sake of performance in so far as it affects forgery resistance. This typically means relying on stronger-than-usual computational assumptions. That is, it's possible that a (pre-quantum) attack might come along that breaks anonymous credit tokens, but not ECDSA, despite the fact that they both use the same elliptic curve. Using fewer hashes PoMFRIT achieved its size record by doing precisely the same thing. Recall that the blind signature requires proving two hash evaluations, one by the client and the other by the issuer. PoMFRIT observes that VOLEitH proof generation can be split into two stages. In the first stage, the client commits to a random mask. It then hashes the message normally (outside of the ZK circuit), combines the result with the mask, and sends the masked target to the issuer. The issuer uses the UOV trapdoor to find a preimage of this target. In the second stage, the client completes the proof that the preimage and previously committed mask are consistent. The hash remains part of the protocol, but the issuer — acting as the VOLEitH verifier — can compute it directly rather than requiring the zero-knowledge proof to reproduce it. This strategy substantially reduces proof size, but it also changes our security posture. The plain UOV assumption is that no (quantum) attacker can find a pre-image for a random target without knowledge of the trapdoor. The corresponding one-more-UOV assumption (analogous to the one-more-MAYO assumption in the PoMFRIT paper ) neatly captures the additional information available to the attacker as a result of this kind of optimization. The assumption, then, is that this additional information doesn't lead to an attack. This assumption may turn out to be overly optimistic. Recently, researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and INRIA managed to forge a 1024-bit RSA signature using a Privacy Pass issuer as a signing oracle. Fortunately, Privacy Pass uses 2048-bit RSA, which, in concert with other defense mechanisms, provides a pretty good security margin. Likewise, for UOV we might consider using NIST Level 3 parameters instead of Level 1. In any case, a bit more study will be required before we rely too heavily on these kinds of optimizations. It's worth emphasizing that a break here would only impact an attacker's ability to forge tokens, not the attacker's ability to violate a client's privacy. Making each hash cheaper Standard SHAKE uses a 1600-bit Keccak state with 24 applications of an underlying round function. However, since the SHA-3 standard was published, many have come to believe that 24 rounds is just too much crypto . TurboSHAKE works the same way, except the permutation uses 12 rounds instead of 24. This substantially reduces the size of VOLEitH proofs. In fact, we're quite comfortable with this security margin, and not just for this application. Another change to Keccak that reduces the proof size is to reduce the size of the state. 256 bits of the state are reserved for the capacity to get 128 bits security. That leaves 1344 bits that can be hashed in one go, which is more than we need. Reducing the state by half to 800 bits leaves us with a rate of 544 bits, which is plenty. On top of that, it even increases the security at the same number of rounds, as an attacker has less to play with. The smaller state means we’re using half the multiplications in our circuit, which reduces the size of the proof. Leaning into multivariate In an ideal world, we could avoid proving conventional hashes altogether by replacing each hash with something that composes more natively with the algebraic structure of our primitives. Indeed, those familiar with Pedersen commitments and their use in elliptic curve cryptography may wonder if commitments can be constructed from multivariate cryptography. This might look something like this : Fix public, random MQ maps F and G and commit to a message m using c=(m+F(r),G(r)) . The advantage of this approach is that the degree of the constraints is the same as the degree of the constraints for the UOV signature. Not only does this make the proof smaller, it makes it far simpler, since we avoid evaluating symmetric crypto in ZK altogether. We experimented with this approach for our application, and it yielded some impressive results. However, it's not at all clear yet if the parameter regime in which multivariate commitments yield an improvement is also secure. Notably, the risk here is not just to unforgeability, but also to client privacy. A lot more study is needed. Another direction is to build an MQ-friendly pseudorandom generator (PRG). For typical VOLEitH parameters, adding an extra witness bit adds ten bits to the proof. There is a neat trick to make this a lot cheaper: only one bit of proof per bit of witness! Instead of using VOLEitH directly, we commit to a (relatively) short key. That key we stretch into a larger bitstream using a PRG with low-degree so that it can be computed cheaply in the circuit. Now, to add a witness bit w , we get one extra bit k from the PRG, and store the bit w XOR k in the proof. There is a performance trade-off: we need to compute the PRG and the witnesses start at degree 2 instead of 1. That especially increases prover time. Also the benefits on proof size only start to pay off when you need a decent number of witness bits. And of course you need a PRG! You can create a PRG using a random MQ instance, but that’s very slow and seems overly conservative. At the other end is the Goldreich PRG, which can be seen as an as-sparse-as-possible MQ PRG. We’d want something in between, but such PRGs haven’t received much study. Is MOLE ready for post-quantum? We already have post-quantum privacy today, so we have some time before we need to have a solution in place, but now is the time to develop alternatives. Multivariate cryptography looks to be a promising basis for easily building a variety of anonymous tokens and credentials. We're currently developing two schemes in this framework: VOLE-IHAT, a candidate for MOLE endorsements, and VOLE-ACT, a candidate for MOLE credentials. Our current cost estimates for these are shown in the table below. The numbers here are subject to change as we analyze and develop these constructions. We use UOV (uov-Ip) in each case, which means the public keys are all 46.6KB. VOLEitH uses the same parameters as FAEST-EM-128s: issuance presentation PoMFRIT (with UOV) <1KB 4.3KB (redemption) VOLE-IHAT 5.6KB 6.5KB (redemption) VOLE-ACT 5.4KB 12.0KB (spend) These numbers are significantly larger than their classical counterparts. This comes as no great surprise, as "PQ is big" is really the main hallmark of the transition across the board. However, replacing RSA blind signatures with PoMFRIT has comparable overhead to replacing ECDSA with ML-DSA. The runtimes of these protocols are also excellent: each operation takes just a few milliseconds with our implementation . (Runtime can be improved by quite a bit, though at the cost of higher communication.) If these numbers hold, then we've already reached an important milestone: the transition to PQ anonymous credentials for the web can now shift from cryptography design to protocol engineering. In other words, we think we can make these numbers work. For example, whereas classical blind signatures might be cheap enough to redeem on every request, we'll have to figure out how to amortize a single redemption over multiple requests. We have some work to do before we get there. First, we need to make sure our protocols are sound, in particular by producing security proofs for them that show they are secure as long as UOV is secure. Second, we need to wait a bit for cryptanalysis of UOV to catch up. We encourage cryptographers to spend time with multivariate cryptography. Once the parameters stabilize, we believe these schemes will find a place in a ton of useful applications. We've only just scratched the surface so far.

The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS.

Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens, which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy.

With 10 years of deployment experience under our belts — using Privacy Pass for applications such as privacy proxies (like iCloud Private Relay) and relays (like Privacy Gateway) — we, along with others, are collaborating to bring the next generation of this technology to the web. One of our goals is to develop more sophisticated tools for managing agentic traffic that would otherwise consume too many resources and degrade performance for human visitors. Another goal is to foster a more open ecosystem by making it easier for more types of clients to participate. Achieving these goals requires developing new capabilities beyond what Privacy Pass offers today.

Given the trajectory, in this post we look at the prospects for post-quantum. In fact, we're in better shape than one might think. Privacy Pass still relies on classical cryptography, like RSA and elliptic curves. This means that a quantum attacker will be able to forge tokens at will and use them to bypass whatever security mechanism the site operator wants to implement (such as rate limiting). On the other hand, Privacy Pass is unconditionally private, meaning no attacker, quantum or not, can link the redemption of a token to its issuance. What's more, the new capabilities we're developing for this new generation of private authentication technology  can and will be instantiated in a way that upholds the same guarantee: your interaction remains private even after Q-day.

This gives us a little breathing room, but we will need an alternative soon. This is an active area of research that has made significant strides in recent years. Still, just as is the case with other aspects of the transition, the primary challenge is the sheer size of post-quantum alternatives: ML-DSA-44 signatures are a whopping 2,420 bytes, while ECDSA-P256 signatures are just 64 bytes. And there's not much hope for drop-in replacements any time soon. Just as for TLS, we'll have to settle for primitives with higher cost and re-engineer our systems to bear this cost.

But what will those primitives be? In this post, we'll explore one potential future for post-quantum privacy on the web, made possible by a recent breakthrough in the design of blind signatures.

What we need to build: a brief look at MOLE

Let's start with an overview of this new technology, which is presently called MOLE ("Moderation Of unLinkable Endorsements"). We'll have much more to say about MOLE later on, but for now we'll highlight the details that are most relevant to cryptography.

One of the core components of Privacy Pass is a blind signature scheme, which allows a client to obtain a signature under an issuer's secret key without revealing to the issuer the message that it signed. The client can then reveal the message and blind signature later on without linking the signature to its issuance.

One type of Privacy Pass token consists of the message and blindly issued signature. To verify the token, the verifier needs the issuer's public key, and so necessarily learns the identity of the issuer. Thus while these tokens protect the identity of the client, they don't protect the identity of the issuer.

Of course, this is exactly what we want for some use cases. The identity of the issuer tells us something about what type of client is connecting to our edge, a signal we use to make decisions in some of our products and for some of our customers. For instance, a client might use a token issued by one of our customers to prove it is authorized to use the customer's VPN product.

However, for many use cases, this is more information than we actually need to make a decision to grant a client access to a resource. Normally we only care that the token was issued by some entity we trust. In fact, MOLE takes this a step further: the token should hide the identity of the issuer altogether so that we can't treat tokens differently based on who issued them. This guarantees equal treatment regardless of the type of client, making it easier for more clients to participate.

This issuer-hiding property is achieved through a new object called an endorsement. An endorsement is issued by an anchor and redeemed by a moderator. Before redemption, the client and moderator agree on an anchor set, the public keys of the anchors trusted by the moderator. During redemption, the client proves it was issued an endorsement by one of the anchors in the anchor set without revealing which one. Upon acceptance, the moderator issues the client the MOLE credential it will use to moderate the client's interaction with the site.

An endorsement can take many forms, but its key property is that it can be redeemed while hiding the identity of the anchor that issued it. There will also be many types of credentials, but because they're intended to be used by a particular moderator, they needn't be anchor-hiding or even publicly verifiable. This means that everything from blind signatures to anonymous credit tokens or anonymous rate-limited credentials can be used to instantiate MOLE credentials.

Now that we have a sense of what we're building, let's look at our options for post quantum.

A feast of cryptography

When designing cryptographic protocols, adaptability and efficiency are often in tension. Sometimes we know exactly what we want to build and can tailor a construction for that purpose; but the more we tailor the protocol for that use case, the harder it becomes to adapt that construction to a different use case.

Adaptability is essential for a system like MOLE. We're not just building one kind of credential system, but many. And the types of credentials we need are likely to change over time, especially on the web where we must constantly adapt to new traffic patterns and attacker behavior. To keep up, we need a set of building blocks that can be composed together into different protocols to meet different requirements.

Most of the post-quantum cryptographic schemes in wide use today come from larger families of constructions, but have been tuned for their particular application. ML-DSA is a good example here: the cryptographic framework from which this scheme was derived can be used to build a variety of things, but to make ML-DSA as compact as possible, its parameters have been carefully tailored to build an efficient and secure digital signature scheme. However, the same parameters would not necessarily be secure for other use cases.

We have come to view this as the central challenge for post-quantum anonymous credentials: to decouple parameter selection from protocol design. Classical credential systems take this for granted: for the most part, protocol designers don't need to think about the parameters of the elliptic curve they're using, allowing even non-experts in the design of elliptic curve cryptography to build useful things with it. Unfortunately, designing efficient post-quantum credentials still requires an enormous amount of expertise.

This situation seems to have changed, however. Earlier this year, we saw a breakthrough that represents a potential sea change for anonymous credentials.

VOLE-in-the-Head

The roots of this breakthrough go back several years. We'll pick up the story three years ago, with the VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) zero-knowledge proof system (Baum et al., Crypto 2023). A zero-knowledge proof system allows one to prove knowledge of a hidden witness, satisfying some public statement while keeping the witness private. For example, a zero-knowledge proof can be used to prove knowledge of an AES key K for which Y=AES(K,X), where X,Y  are public. This proof can be transformed into a digital signature whose security reduces to the security of AES, with X,Y as the public key and K as the secret key. This is exactly the FAEST digital signature, a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature competition.

Compared to many contemporary proof systems, VOLEitH is relatively simple to understand and implement securely. VOLE stands for "Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation" and is an interactive technique that gives two parties correlated random values. These correlations act like authentication tags, allowing the verifier to check that a computation on the hidden witness was performed correctly. In VOLEitH, the prover prepares locally what the two parties would normally generate together — hence “in the head” — then commits to those values and uses the Fiat-Shamir transformation (a widely used tool in cryptography) to select the parts the verifier checks. This step turns the interactive VOLE process into a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof.

Apart from its simplicity, VOLEitH is a fairly unremarkable proof system. It's not succinct in the way many other proof systems are: its proofs are asymptotically linear in the size of the witness and the arithmetic complexity of the statement being proved. However, VOLEitH is concretely very efficient for a particular type of statement, namely one that can be expressed as a set of equations over small binary fields.

One example is the relation Y=AES(K,X) we just discussed. We don't normally think of AES as a set of equations, but many of its computations are designed around arithmetic in GF(28), a field whose elements are single bytes. FAEST proofs for this statement are only about 4KB (NIST Round 3, 128s).

Another example is the KuMQuat signature scheme, in which the signer proves an instance of the Multivariate Quadratic (MQ) problem. Here we're given a system of random, quadratic equations of multiple variables over a small field, like GF(28). Mathematically, this MQ map P looks something like P(s) = (sTA1s + b1s,…,sTAms + bms) where s and each bi are length n vectors and each Ai is an n-by-n matrix. Given P,P(s) for random s, the MQ problem is to find s. We call it quadratic because we multiply the elements of s by itself.

The MQ problem is believed to be hard to solve even for a quantum computer. But because P is made up of quadratic equations, proving knowledge of a solution with VOLEitH is fairly cheap, yielding KuMQuat signatures as small as 2.6KB.

When compared to other post-quantum signatures like ML-DSA or FN-DSA, these numbers don't look especially impressive. But how VOLEitH compares to other schemes in a particular category of constructions is beside the point. For MOLE, we'll need to strike a balance between performance and the ability to build many types of credential systems. To that end, we need one more ingredient.

Multivariate signatures

Another way to build signatures from MQ maps involves embedding some additional mathematical structure into the map. In the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) signature scheme, the public key is an MQ map P, and a signature is a vector s satisfying P(s) = t, where t is obtained by hashing and salting the message to be signed.

In the public key, oil and vinegar variables are mixed together in a way that hides this structure in the map.
