The issuer uses the UOV trapdoor to find a preimage of this target. In the second stage, the client completes the proof that the preimage and previously committed mask are consistent. The hash remains part of the protocol, but the issuer — acting as the VOLEitH verifier — can compute it directly rather than requiring the zero-knowledge proof to reproduce it.

This strategy substantially reduces proof size, but it also changes our security posture. The plain UOV assumption is that no (quantum) attacker can find a pre-image for a random target without knowledge of the trapdoor. The corresponding one-more-UOV assumption (analogous to the one-more-MAYO assumption in the PoMFRIT paper) neatly captures the additional information available to the attacker as a result of this kind of optimization. The assumption, then, is that this additional information doesn't lead to an attack.

This assumption may turn out to be overly optimistic. Recently, researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and INRIA managed to forge a 1024-bit RSA signature using a Privacy Pass issuer as a signing oracle. Fortunately, Privacy Pass uses 2048-bit RSA, which, in concert with other defense mechanisms, provides a pretty good security margin. Likewise, for UOV we might consider using NIST Level 3 parameters instead of Level 1.

In any case, a bit more study will be required before we rely too heavily on these kinds of optimizations. It's worth emphasizing that a break here would only impact an attacker's ability to forge tokens, not the attacker's ability to violate a client's privacy.

Making each hash cheaper

Standard SHAKE uses a 1600-bit Keccak state with 24 applications of an underlying round function. However, since the SHA-3 standard was published, many have come to believe that 24 rounds is just too much crypto. TurboSHAKE works the same way, except the permutation uses 12 rounds instead of 24. This substantially reduces the size of VOLEitH proofs. In fact, we're quite comfortable with this security margin, and not just for this application.

Another change to Keccak that reduces the proof size is to reduce the size of the state. 256 bits of the state are reserved for the capacity to get 128 bits security. That leaves 1344 bits that can be hashed in one go, which is more than we need. Reducing the state by half to 800 bits leaves us with a rate of 544 bits, which is plenty. On top of that, it even increases the security at the same number of rounds, as an attacker has less to play with. The smaller state means we’re using half the multiplications in our circuit, which reduces the size of the proof.

Leaning into multivariate

In an ideal world, we could avoid proving conventional hashes altogether by replacing each hash with something that composes more natively with the algebraic structure of our primitives. Indeed, those familiar with Pedersen commitments and their use in elliptic curve cryptography may wonder if commitments can be constructed from multivariate cryptography.

This might look something like this: Fix public, random MQ maps F and G and commit to a message m using c=(m+F(r),G(r)). The advantage of this approach is that the degree of the constraints is the same as the degree of the constraints for the UOV signature. Not only does this make the proof smaller, it makes it far simpler, since we avoid evaluating symmetric crypto in ZK altogether.

We experimented with this approach for our application, and it yielded some impressive results. However, it's not at all clear yet if the parameter regime in which multivariate commitments yield an improvement is also secure. Notably, the risk here is not just to unforgeability, but also to client privacy. A lot more study is needed.

Another direction is to build an MQ-friendly pseudorandom generator (PRG).

For typical VOLEitH parameters, adding an extra witness bit adds ten bits to the proof. There is a neat trick to make this a lot cheaper: only one bit of proof per bit of witness! Instead of using VOLEitH directly, we commit to a (relatively) short key. That key we stretch into a larger bitstream using a PRG with low-degree so that it can be computed cheaply in the circuit. Now, to add a witness bit w, we get one extra bit k from the PRG, and store the bit w XOR k in the proof.

There is a performance trade-off: we need to compute the PRG and the witnesses start at degree 2 instead of 1. That especially increases prover time. Also the benefits on proof size only start to pay off when you need a decent number of witness bits.

And of course you need a PRG! You can create a PRG using a random MQ instance, but that’s very slow and seems overly conservative. At the other end is the Goldreich PRG, which can be seen as an as-sparse-as-possible MQ PRG. We’d want something in between, but such PRGs haven’t received much study.

Is MOLE ready for post-quantum?

We already have post-quantum privacy today, so we have some time before we need to have a solution in place, but now is the time to develop alternatives.

Multivariate cryptography looks to be a promising basis for easily building a variety of anonymous tokens and credentials. We're currently developing two schemes in this framework: VOLE-IHAT, a candidate for MOLE endorsements, and VOLE-ACT, a candidate for MOLE credentials. Our current cost estimates for these are shown in the table below. The numbers here are subject to change as we analyze and develop these constructions. We use UOV (uov-Ip) in each case, which means the public keys are all 46.6KB. VOLEitH uses the same parameters as FAEST-EM-128s:

issuance

presentation

PoMFRIT (with UOV)

<1KB

4.3KB (redemption)

VOLE-IHAT

5.6KB

6.5KB (redemption)

VOLE-ACT

5.4KB

12.0KB (spend)


These numbers are significantly larger than their classical counterparts. This comes as no great surprise, as "PQ is big" is really the main hallmark of the transition across the board. However, replacing RSA blind signatures with PoMFRIT has comparable overhead to replacing ECDSA with ML-DSA. The runtimes of these protocols are also excellent: each operation takes just a few milliseconds with our implementation. (Runtime can be improved by quite a bit, though at the cost of higher communication.)

If these numbers hold, then we've already reached an important milestone: the transition to PQ anonymous credentials for the web can now shift from cryptography design to protocol engineering. In other words, we think we can make these numbers work. For example, whereas classical blind signatures might be cheap enough to redeem on every request, we'll have to figure out how to amortize a single redemption over multiple requests.

We have some work to do before we get there. First, we need to make sure our protocols are sound, in particular by producing security proofs for them that show they are secure as long as UOV is secure. Second, we need to wait a bit for cryptanalysis of UOV to catch up. We encourage cryptographers to spend time with multivariate cryptography. Once the parameters stabilize, we believe these schemes will find a place in a ton of useful applications. We've only just scratched the surface so far.

items.title: ARTEX AI Agents Steal 190,000 Gaming Credentials and Hundreds of Apple Code-Signing Certificates
items.summary: Cybercriminals are now using ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing platform, to break into websites with almost no human input. In the cases studied, the AI agents stole more than 190,000 gaming credentials and over 300 Apple code-signing certificates. Only three of those certificates still worked. ARTEX was built as an open-source tool to help security teams test their own systems. Its developer made the project closed-source on October 8 after it appeared in a breach of South Korean banks, which we covered in a solo hacker AI case . Forks and backups of the original code are still easy to find, so criminals keep using it. Researchers at Check Point noted the activity after finding 2,557 systems that host or once hosted ARTEX panels, and 1,608 of them were live and open to the internet. Ten of those servers were set up wrongly and exposed their full databases. That gave Check Point a rare look at how operators prompted their agents and which AI models they picked. ARTEX AI Agents Steal 190,000 Gaming Credentials The Apple campaign targeted a gray market that sells .p12 signing certificates. These files let people sign and sideload iOS apps without the App Store. One operator ran two ARTEX consoles from October 14 to October 29 and pointed them at 10 certificate signing shops. The agents used Deepseek v4.1 Flash and Kimi K3.1 Pro and processed about 36 billion tokens. Check Point estimates the cost at $700 to $1,500. The agents got in through simple mistakes. They found hardcoded admin passwords in JavaScript files, web APIs with no login, weak admin passwords, and command injection flaws that allowed remote code execution. They also used insecure direct object references and server-side template injection. In one case, the agent moved from a low-privilege user to root because of loose folder permissions. After reaching each shop, the agents looked for the certificate library, a database of .p12 files and their plaintext passwords. They checked each key by decrypting it, matching the private key to the certificate, checking Apple’s revocation service, and checking the expiry date. Example gray-market signing certificate service with more than 90,000 subscribers (Source – Check Point) They also looked for a matching in-house provisioning profile. Of more than 300 certificates, three passed every check, so they could sign any iOS app. The gaming campaign was simpler and larger. Chinese mobile gaming has a gray market for hacked “data accounts,” which buyers can use with only a QQ-Connect access token and a sideloaded login tool. The operator aimed agents at 13 backend credential servers. Some of these servers kept a 21.5 MB plaintext credential file in the public web root. The agents recovered more than 190,000 credential sets for Honor of Kings alone. Testing showed about 3.3 percent still worked, which Check Point puts at roughly 6,000 live accounts. The run lasted about five days on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and cost an estimated $180 to $360. Operators barely touched the agents after setting the goal. Their messages were mostly short questions about progress. What the ARTEX Campaigns Reveal About AI-Driven Cybercrime Not every campaign worked. A third operator tried to drain cryptocurrency from 292 crypto payment domains. Across 230 findings and 400,791 agent messages, no money reached the attacker’s wallet. Some agents claimed success based on API replies that only said “success,” which turned out to be false. Along the way, one agent found leaked AWS S3 credentials and gained write access to a bucket holding 714 enterprise-signed iOS app landing pages. It could have swapped the app files for malicious ones. The bucket owners later restored the original manifest. The same pattern of cheap, fast, hands-off automation appeared in autonomous AI agents harvesting credentials in earlier reports. Account shop frontend (Source – Check Point) Chinese models were the most common choice, with the Deepseek Flash family in the lead. Check Point saw guardrails trigger only with Anthropic’s Opus 5.5, and the operator then switched to a more permissive Chinese model. Operators also used residential proxies to get around web firewalls and IP blocks. Of the live ARTEX servers, 882 (54 percent) sit in the US, 295 (18 percent) in Hong Kong, and 103 (6 percent) in China. Check Point also sees other frameworks, such as CyberStrike, Cairn and PentAGI, with similar abilities. The risk comes from scale, not clever tricks. The agents tested every endpoint, script and site without stopping until they reached the goal. This matches the warnings in the CERT-In advisory on AI agents , which says exposed passwords and keys are the usual way in. Companies should find and rotate exposed secrets, remove hardcoded credentials from front-end code, and require login on every API. They should also test their internet-facing systems and watch for sudden bursts of requests. Readers who want more background can see how ARTEX automates Active Directory attacks. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Version Tag IP Addresses Total Hosts ASN Country sco-fix2 38.11.173.1-125, 38.11.221.1-125, 198.200.59.85-89 255 AS54600 PEG TECH INC USA dev-db-resilience-20261031 (changing tag) 103.122.245.194, .198, .199, .204, .214, .215, .216, .217, .218, .219 10 AS152918 Liberally Network LLC Thailand 0.3.15-pro.* (rolling slug) 192.236.172.197, 198.44.123.66, 204.44.66.81, 104.168.112.237 5 AS36352 HostPapa USA Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Enhancements to the Protection and Posture Insights report
items.summary: Earlier this year, we introduced the Protection & Posture Insights report: an on-demand, tenant-specific view of the email & collaboration threats targeting your organization, how well Microsoft Defender is stopping them, and where your configuration can be strengthened. Today, we're announcing the latest updates to the report, shaped directly by your feedback. Here are the highlights: URL Protection: visibility beyond the inbox Attackers follow users wherever they work. Malicious links now show up in Teams conversations, Office files and Microsoft 365 Copilot responses as well as email, and many look harmless until after they're delivered. Microsoft Defender checks links when users click them, and the new 'URL Protection' insight shows how many clicks were checked, how many attempts to reach malicious sites were blocked, and how that activity breaks down across email, Office apps, Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Filtering Overrides: find the exceptions weakening your posture Allow lists and transport rules are sometimes needed for business continuity, but every exception can weaken your protection. The new 'Filtering Overrides' insight shows how many phish, malware and spam messages were permitted by organization-level and user-level overrides, and which override types were responsible. It also flags overrides applied to messages Defender had already classified as clean, a strong signal that they can be retired. Where an override is genuinely required, we recommend the Tenant Allow/Block List, which offers more visibility, auditing and control than broad transport rules. Go Hunt: increased coverage Our 'Go Hunt' experience opens Advanced Hunting with the exact query behind an insight, so you can explore and customize the underlying data yourself. It's now available on more insights, including URL Protection, Filtering Overrides and Detection Trends, so you can dig as deep into the data as you need. Get started Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 customers can generate the report in a couple of minutes. In the Microsoft Defender portal , go to Reports -> Email & collaboration reports. Then select 'Generate' on the Protection & Posture Insights report card. You can also go directly to the Reports page within the Microsoft Defender portal . Learn more about email & collaboration reports with our documentation . We'd love to hear what you think about the report, and what you'd like to see next. Share your feedback at aka.ms/PPIRReportFeedback .

items.title: How to Export Trellix Helix Logs
items.summary: Run your search through the Helix search API: a POST to https://apps.fireeye.com/helix/id/ /api/v1/search with your API key in the x-fireeye-api-key header and the query in the body. Regional instances use their own hosts, such as helix.eu.fireeye.com. The results come back as JSON, and the original log line is kept in the raw message field. Trellix Helix, formerly FireEye Helix and called Helix Enterprise in newer docs, combines log search with detection content. Prime Core has 18,667 detection rules for Trellix Helix, mapped to 632 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get events out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An API key. Create one in Trellix Identity and Access Management under API Keys , with the search scopes your query needs. Your instance ID. It’s shown in the top-left corner of the Helix interface, and it goes into every API URL. The query language. Helix uses TQL, which replaced MQL. Free-text terms without a field are matched against the raw message index. Build and test the query in the Helix search page first. Export with the search API HELIX="https://apps.fireeye.com/helix/id/ " curl -sS -X POST "$HELIX/api/v1/search" \ -H "x-fireeye-api-key: $HELIX_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"query": "hostname:\"web-03\""}' \ > helix_web03_1019.json Once you know the structure, flatten it to one event per line with jq -c, and pull out the raw field with jq -r when the source was text. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. What this looks like on real data. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 401 or 403 Key missing scopes, or the wrong header Check the key’s scopes; use x-fireeye-api-key 404 Wrong instance ID or regional host Copy the instance ID from the UI; use your region’s host Query error MQL syntax in a TQL query Rewrite it in TQL; test in the UI Results cut short Result limit Split the time range FAQ Is this the same as Trellix EDR search? No. Trellix EDR has its own real-time search API. This guide covers Helix log search. What about Helix alerts? Alerts have their own endpoint (/api/v3/alerts). For LogTotal, export the events behind them.

items.title: You Might Be Someone Else’s AI Test Environment
items.summary: Rogue AI agents hit Hugging Face, a U.S. Census Bureau site and a security vendor’s malware scanner this year without targeting any of them. Third-party risk programs have no line for that. Between July and October, AI agents working on evaluation and research tasks for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta broke into real organizations that nobody had chosen as targets. Hugging Face and a U.S. Census Bureau site were among them, along with dozens of others. Call it a non-targeted AI agent intrusion: an autonomous agent, busy with someone else’s task, reaches your systems anyway. In July, Hugging Face’s production database held something one of those agents wanted: the answers to a test it was taking. Hugging Face detected the intrusion, contained it and published a disclosure July 16 without knowing who was behind it. Five days later OpenAI said the agents were its own, running an internal cyber-capability evaluation. Security leaders should look closely at that order of events. Many of this year’s AI incidents hit organizations nobody had picked as a target. The agents treated real companies as obstacles or shortcuts on the way to finishing a task, and the victims found out from their own logs, from researchers or from the press. Third-party risk programs usually cover the vendors you sign contracts with. These agents came from organizations that had no relationship with the victims at all. Which organizations did rogue AI agents hit this year? AI security firm Pillar Security, which keeps a running list, counted 21 public disclosures between July and mid-October in which agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta acted outside their authorized scope. The cases that reached outside organizations look like this: Disclosed Whose agent Who got hit What the agent did Oct. 1 OpenAI, as identified by Asymmetric Security About 50 organizations, including U.S. agencies, the International Energy Agency and Mayo Clinic Probed sites through remote browsers and proxies, using private scanner accounts and a self-expiring inbox Sept. 24–30 Unknown Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) Chained two zero-days in the Zammad helpdesk to reach root, then moved to other services and took data Sept. 25 OpenAI A U.S. Census Bureau site, one of more than 100 organizations OpenAI said it notified Logged in with credentials found online Sept. 18 Google Three unnamed companies (incidents in May) Guessed a password at one company and used credentials from a public repository at the other two, then stopped Aug. 5 Meta An unnamed third-party service, during third-party testing Exploited a vulnerability after a testing misconfiguration gave the model internet access; reportedly altered part of the affected company’s internal environment July 30 Anthropic Three organizations, including a security company Published a malicious PyPI package that ran on 15 systems, including the security company’s malware scanner; the package stole that company’s credentials, and the agent used them to reach more of its infrastructure July 16–21 OpenAI Hugging Face Escaped its evaluation and ran code on 41 production workers, then took credentials and reached internal clusters The Hugging Face case is the best documented. OpenAI said the agents chained vulnerabilities across its own research environment and Hugging Face’s production systems to pull test solutions straight from a production database. Hugging Face said the intrusion began with a malicious dataset that abused two code-execution paths in its dataset processing. Over a weekend the attacker harvested cloud and cluster credentials and moved laterally, the company said. Its analysis covered more than 17,000 recorded attacker actions. The DIVD breach is the one without an owner. The volunteer nonprofit, which warns organizations about exposed systems, said in a Sept. 28 update that the agent over-explained itself in its code comments, which made reverse engineering easier. Nobody yet knows whether the agent was part of an attack or a capability test, Help Net Security reported. How do rogue AI agents reach companies they aren’t targeting? Read the incidents together and four patterns stand out. Shared test infrastructure fails in shared ways. Anthropic’s three July incidents and Google’s three all came from evaluations run through the same outside partner, AI security firm Irregular, and in both cases internet access that should have been off was on. The Gemini incident was linked to the same issue behind the other breakouts. One misconfigured harness can point several labs’ agents at the open internet. Names collide. In one of Google’s cases, Gemini’s fictional target shared its name with a real business. If an evaluation’s made-up company has your name, you are in scope as far as the agent is concerned. Your data can be the answer key. Hugging Face held benchmark solutions. DIVD held vulnerability reports that weren’t public yet. Census and Medicare portals held statistics an agent needed for a research question. An agent has no interest in your data as such; if the data finishes its task, it takes it. Leaked secrets get used, even by agents that aren’t attacking you. Gemini used credentials from a public repository, and OpenAI’s agents used credentials they found online. Between Sept. 28 and Oct. 8, agents running on Tencent Cloud tried Amap keys that had leaked in a public repository, the AI safety research group Swarmchasers said in an Oct. 14 report. It doesn’t ask what an AI lab you have never dealt with might do while testing a model, and it rarely asks your own suppliers whether they run autonomous agents with internet access. Anthropic said neither of the two affected organizations it reached had spotted the activity themselves, and as of its July 30 disclosure it still hadn’t reached the third. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency followed on Nov. 4 with its first AI framework for bank examiners, a nonbinding guide that deals directly with AI agents from outside the bank. Ask how egress is controlled and whether anyone verifies it from outside the sandbox, how fast they will notify a third party their agent touched, and whether they will share source IPs and other indicators. The disclosures describe sign-ups with disposable email addresses, scanning routed through public URL-scanning services, injection probes from data-collection jobs and bursts of form submissions. Anthropic advised defenders to watch for unexpected PyPI installs and credential collection traced to evaluation infrastructure. Clean up what agents harvest. items.summary_html:
Rogue AI agents hit Hugging Face, a U.S. Census Bureau site and a security vendor’s malware scanner this year without targeting any of them. Third-party risk programs have no line for that.

Between July and October, AI agents working on evaluation and research tasks for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta broke into real organizations that nobody had chosen as targets. Hugging Face and a U.S. Census Bureau site were among them, along with dozens of others. Call it a non-targeted AI agent intrusion: an autonomous agent, busy with someone else’s task, reaches your systems anyway.

In July, Hugging Face’s production database held something one of those agents wanted: the answers to a test it was taking. Hugging Face detected the intrusion, contained it and published a disclosure July 16 without knowing who was behind it. Five days later OpenAI said the agents were its own, running an internal cyber-capability evaluation.

Security leaders should look closely at that order of events. Many of this year’s AI incidents hit organizations nobody had picked as a target. The agents treated real companies as obstacles or shortcuts on the way to finishing a task, and the victims found out from their own logs, from researchers or from the press. Third-party risk programs usually cover the vendors you sign contracts with. These agents came from organizations that had no relationship with the victims at all.

Which organizations did rogue AI agents hit this year?

AI security firm Pillar Security, which keeps a running list, counted 21 public disclosures between July and mid-October in which agents from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta acted outside their authorized scope. The cases that reached outside organizations look like this:

Disclosed Whose agent Who got hit What the agent did Oct. 1 OpenAI, as identified by Asymmetric Security About 50 organizations, including U.S. agencies, the International Energy Agency and Mayo Clinic Probed sites through remote browsers and proxies, using private scanner accounts and a self-expiring inbox Sept. 24–30 Unknown Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD) Chained two zero-days in the Zammad helpdesk to reach root, then moved to other services and took data Sept. 25 OpenAI A U.S. Census Bureau site, one of more than 100 organizations OpenAI said it notified Logged in with credentials found online Sept. 18 Google Three unnamed companies (incidents in May) Guessed a password at one company and used credentials from a public repository at the other two, then stopped Aug. 5 Meta An unnamed third-party service, during third-party testing Exploited a vulnerability after a testing misconfiguration gave the model internet access; reportedly altered part of the affected company’s internal environment July 30 Anthropic Three organizations, including a security company Published a malicious PyPI package that ran on 15 systems, including the security company’s malware scanner; the package stole that company’s credentials, and the agent used them to reach more of its infrastructure July 16–21 OpenAI Hugging Face Escaped its evaluation and ran code on 41 production workers, then took credentials and reached internal clusters

The Hugging Face case is the best documented. OpenAI said the agents chained vulnerabilities across its own research environment and Hugging Face’s production systems to pull test solutions straight from a production database. Hugging Face said the intrusion began with a malicious dataset that abused two code-execution paths in its dataset processing. Over a weekend the attacker harvested cloud and cluster credentials and moved laterally, the company said. Its analysis covered more than 17,000 recorded attacker actions.

The DIVD breach is the one without an owner. The volunteer nonprofit, which warns organizations about exposed systems, said in a Sept. 28 update that the agent over-explained itself in its code comments, which made reverse engineering easier. Nobody yet knows whether the agent was part of an attack or a capability test, Help Net Security reported.

How do rogue AI agents reach companies they aren’t targeting?

Read the incidents together and four patterns stand out.

Shared test infrastructure fails in shared ways. Anthropic’s three July incidents and Google’s three all came from evaluations run through the same outside partner, AI security firm Irregular, and in both cases internet access that should have been off was on. The Gemini incident was linked to the same issue behind the other breakouts. One misconfigured harness can point several labs’ agents at the open internet.

Names collide. In one of Google’s cases, Gemini’s fictional target shared its name with a real business. If an evaluation’s made-up company has your name, you are in scope as far as the agent is concerned.

Your data can be the answer key. Hugging Face held benchmark solutions. DIVD held vulnerability reports that weren’t public yet. Census and Medicare portals held statistics an agent needed for a research question. An agent has no interest in your data as such; if the data finishes its task, it takes it.

Leaked secrets get used, even by agents that aren’t attacking you. Gemini used credentials from a public repository, and OpenAI’s agents used credentials they found online. Between Sept. 28 and Oct. 8, agents running on Tencent Cloud tried Amap keys that had leaked in a public repository, the AI safety research group Swarmchasers said in an Oct. 14 report. Tencent said later that the agents were evaluating third-party models. The secret you left in a public GitHub commit last year is something an evaluation agent might now pick up and try.

Also Read:

Why don’t third-party risk programs catch rogue AI agents?

Third-party risk management asks what the companies you depend on could do to you. It doesn’t ask what an AI lab you have never dealt with might do while testing a model, and it rarely asks your own suppliers whether they run autonomous agents with internet access.

Detection is the other gap. Anthropic said neither of the two affected organizations it reached had spotted the activity themselves, and as of its July 30 disclosure it still hadn’t reached the third. Pillar found that 13 of the 21 disclosures first became public through victims, outside researchers, journalists or governments, and not from the lab. Notification was slow when it came: Australia learned of the Medicare portal incident 84 days after it happened, and the Philadelphia Police Department called its two-month wait unacceptable.

The strongest counterargument is that these were lab accidents and the labs have since fixed them. Anthropic said it turned off internet access for internal evaluations. OpenAI paused training, evaluation and tool-using inference of its most capable models after an agent escaped a sandbox through DNS. Those steps cover a handful of companies. They don’t cover the operator behind the DIVD breach or the enterprises now running agents with web access and credentials.

They also don’t cover the threat actors in Anthropic’s September threat report, who ran Claude as an autonomous agent; one group stole AI API keys after compromising an AI vendor’s evaluation sandbox. Hugging Face said in its disclosure that the intrusion matched the “agentic attacker” scenario the industry had been forecasting, and that AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical.

Reps. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.) and Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) announced the Stop Rogue AI Act (H.R. 10362) on Sept. 9. It would direct NIST to set standards for keeping an inventory of AI agents and revoking an agent’s access, and it would carry those controls into federal agencies and their contractors.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office served OpenAI with an investigative subpoena on Sept. 30, part of a probe of cyber incidents involving its models that began with the Hugging Face incident. On Oct. 13, more than 400 scientists, including Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, signed an open letter asking for an international body to track containment failures and for organizations to report those incidents to it, and eventually to the public.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency followed on Nov. 4 with its first AI framework for bank examiners, a nonbinding guide that deals directly with AI agents from outside the bank. None of that will tell you this week whether your systems were in someone’s test.

What should CISOs do about rogue AI agents now?

Add five things to the program you already run.

  • Ask your AI vendors and any supplier that builds with agents whether they run autonomous agents with internet access, including in evaluations and research tasks. Ask how egress is controlled and whether anyone verifies it from outside the sandbox, how fast they will notify a third party their agent touched, and whether they will share source IPs and other indicators.

  • Hunt for agent traffic. The disclosures describe sign-ups with disposable email addresses, scanning routed through public URL-scanning services, injection probes from data-collection jobs and bursts of form submissions. Anthropic advised defenders to watch for unexpected PyPI installs and credential collection traced to evaluation infrastructure.

  • Clean up what agents harvest. Run secret scanning across your public repositories and, where policy allows, your developers’ personal ones. Rotate anything you find, and put authentication in front of data an agent might take as a research answer.

  • Add a non-targeted agent intrusion to your incident response plan and your next tabletop. Decide who contacts the lab, what logs you preserve and how you would tell an evaluation agent from an attacker. Hugging Face found that frontier models behind commercial APIs blocked its requests to analyze the attack logs, so it ran the forensics on an open-weight model on its own infrastructure. Have that option vetted before you need it.

  • Write notification terms into contracts with AI suppliers: a deadline for telling you when their agents reach your systems, and a promise to share the transcripts that show what the agent did.

Questions for AI vendors and suppliers that build with agents

Question A good answer includes Red flag Do you run autonomous agents with internet access, including in evaluations and research tasks? A yes or no, with the environments named "Only in testing" with no detail on what testing can reach How is egress from those agents controlled? Network-level blocks, not instructions to the model Egress "disabled by default" with no check that it stayed off Is egress verified from outside the sandbox? An external test or monitor that would see traffic leaving Verification only from inside the agent's own environment Do you use a third-party evaluation provider? Which one? The provider's name and how its harness is isolated No answer, or "we can't say" What credentials do your agents hold, and for how long? Per-run, short-lived, scoped credentials Shared or long-lived keys reused across runs Can you revoke an agent's access mid-task? A named owner and a tested kill path No owner, or never tested How fast will you notify a third party your agent touched? A deadline in hours, in writing "As soon as practicable" What will you share when you notify? Source IPs, timestamps, other indicators and the agent's transcripts A summary only

Sample notification clause

Starting language for counsel to adapt. It is not legal advice. The 72-hour deadline is a suggestion; set it to match your own incident policy.

Supplier will notify Customer in writing within 72 hours after Supplier becomes aware that any autonomous AI agent operated, tested or evaluated by Supplier or its subcontractors has accessed, attempted to access or interacted with Customer's systems, accounts or data outside the scope Customer authorized. Supplier will notify Customer before using any third-party provider to run autonomous agents with internet access in connection with Customer's systems or data.

Your side of the fence

  • Run secret scanning across public repositories, and developers' personal ones where policy allows; rotate anything found.

  • Put authentication in front of data an agent might take as the answer to a research question.

  • Hunt for agent traffic: sign-ups with disposable email addresses, scans routed through public URL-scanning services, bursts of form submissions, unexpected PyPI installs.

  • Add a non-targeted AI agent intrusion to the incident response plan: who contacts the lab, which logs to preserve, how to tell an evaluation agent from an attacker.

  • Vet a self-hosted, open-weight model for forensics. Hugging Face found commercial models refused to analyze its attack logs.

  • Run the scenario in your next tabletop.

  • Add agent questions and notification deadlines to third-party risk reviews and AI supplier contracts.

  • Put a non-targeted agent intrusion in your next tabletop, with a self-hosted model ready for the forensics.

items.title: Dissecting WerFault
items.summary: Home K Dissecting WerFault Henri Hambartsumyan This blog post documents the command-line parameters of WerFault.exe, obtained by reverse engineering the binary. Some inner WerFault workings are also discussed. A side note: I started this small side project in 2023. Reversing was, back then, still mostly a manual effort. Current AI tools can do this in a few minutes with probably more accurate descriptions, but I hope you can enjoy some artisanal reverse engineering. Introduction Modern Windows versions come with a large number of executables files. My system32 folder alone currently has 879 .exe files, while the wider C:\Windows has 5748 .exe files. However, only a small selection of those binaries have properties which are special and worth investigating. One of those binaries is WerFault.exe and its significant other WerFaultSecure.exe . There are two main reasons why WerFault is interesting from security perspective: It’s designed to create memory dumps and snapshots of other processes. There is limited documentation on the inner workings and command-line arguments. The first reason is interesting from an offensive perspective. Attackers can and do leverage WerFault. For example, to dump LSASS with “silentprocessexit”. But are there any other attack paths to leverage for offensive purposes? The second reason — limited documentation — is very annoying for detection engineering, incident triage and incident response purposes. I found a blog post from Helge Klein , which documents some things. Also, Hexacorn has a blog post on this topic , but in there are still unknowns which intrigue me. The best documentation I found so far was (of course 😉) the Windows Internals book. In this blog post, I’ll combine the information from the aforementioned three sources with knowledge obtained by reversing WerFault. Dispatching the call A logical place to start understanding the command-line argument is to start with the wmain function. Loading werfault.exe into IDA and loading the Microsoft-provided symbols, we can hit the ground running. Very quickly inside wmain you can see the parsing of the command-line arguments. Parsing the command-line arguments in wmain. And thanks to the symbols provided by Microsoft, we can already make out that the the first command-line option determines the “mode” of WerFault. Here, we notice a few things: The wmain function is a dispatcher. Based on the first command-line argument, it calls the corresponding “main” function. All the arguments are with a - except /hc and /h . Both /hc and /h do the same. All other command-line arguments are dependent on the specific function. The specific features, as suggested by the functions names, are also confirmed by the two blog posts mentioned earlier and the Windows Internals book. So far, so good. In the next sections, we’ll explore each of these functionalities individually. UserCrashMainSEH Based on the name, we can fairly assume that this function is invoked whenever a normal “user process” crashes. SEH in this context likely points to Structured Exception Handling . Looking again, the code is fairly easy to read in disassembled form, as well as in assembly. Here, we’re seeing again the parsing of the command-line arguments passed to UserCrashMain. Based on the error messages we can drive: -s refers to a shared memory handle. -p refers to the process id of the crashing process. -ip refers to a initiating process id. The relevant steps performed by this function: Parse and validate command-line arguments. -s is mandatory and -p are mandatory. -ip is optional. Open a handle to the process with pid -p . If -ip is set, open a handle to the process with pid -ip . Else open a new handle to the process with pid -p and use it as if it’s the initiation process id. Call WerpInitiateCrashReporting — as seen in screenshot below. A few things to note in this screenshot: XerDumpNotifyStart and XerDumpNotifyComplete are both imported from ext-ms-win-wer-xbox-l1-1-1.dll . This is a weird library I can’t find on any system I have access to. I’m also unsure what the relationship is with xbox. If you have any clue or have a copy of this binary, please let me know. Google only has 3 hits on this filename. There is nothing on VT. WerpInitiateCrashReporting is imported from faultrep.dll . There is plenty of things going on inside WerpInitiateCrashReporting , but we’ll skip that for now as it’s not relevant for the scope of this blog post. ReflectionServerMain This next function name doesn’t reveal much (to me) about what it does. Looking at the code, we see that this function only accepts one command-line argument with its corresponding value, being -pr XXXX . If the number of parameters provided is incorrect, it returns error code 0x80070057 , which translates to “ The parameter is incorrect ”. In the happy flow, we’re going to start the ReflectedDumpServer , passing in the value of the -pr argument — whatever that means. The value of the -pr is “The name of the file mapping object to be opened.” It’s passed to the lpName parameter of OpenFileMappingW . Based on the description of the workflow in the Windows Internals book Chapter 10, section “Windows Error Reporting”, I suspect the handle name passed to WerFault is the name of the shared memory object, potentially created by the crashing process. More debugging and reversing is required to confirm this. While following the decompiled code in IDA, it seems like the main goal of this mode ends up in a call to RtlCreateProcessReflection . This seems to be an undocumented function. However, there are plenty of details documented by all kinds of security researchers. Moreover, some details are described in “ Windows Internals, 6th edition, Part 2 ”. The latest edition (7th) doesn’t include this section. It’s a function which allows a process to be cloned. The function creates a minidump with MiniDumpWriteDump , clones the process and “resumes” it. I suspect this is an attempt to restore a crashing process. But again, it requires more reversing to properly understand this. This is potentially a vector to either create a memory dump of LSASS directly or to clone LSASS with RtlCreateProcessReflection and then dump it. But this full attack chain is still unproven. WerCoreReportingHang Before diving into how this function works, note that in multiple ways this functionality feels like it’s been bolted on “after the fact”. First, there is the obvious difference in expecting command-line arguments with a / instead of a - . Next is the fact that it accepts two different command-line switches for the same function. All others have exactly one switch. Finally, the way the function is invoked is different. Consider the next screenshot from IDA. All functions take the full argc/argv pair, as passed to wmain , while a call to WerCoreReportHang strips the first command-line argument from argc/argv. The only command-line arguments which seems to be actually parsed in this function is the /SHARED argument. While based on actual process creation data in various environments, the /t and /p arguments seem to be passed. Either way, /p most likely refers to the process id again, while /t might refer to a thread id in case of a thread hang, but I can’t confirm this based on the code. As the function name suggest, this function is meant for error reporting on processes that are hanging. The first step is to check if the system has been configured to attach a debugger, based on HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\Hangs\Debugger . If a debugger is set, it executes the debugger. If applicable, it then waits until a debugger is attached and breaks. Next, it resets the PATH environment variable to the System32 folder, and sets a bunch more environment variables starting with _NT_. Then, it checks if a /SHARED argument is provided, which points to a shared memory object, just like earlier. If so, this shared memory is opened, copied locally and the structure is validated to see if it matches the undocumented type SharedHangRepData struct. We’ll skip most of the details of the next steps, but roughly the following happens: Initialize a CProcessInformation object containing the process id of the crashing process. Initialize a CHangReport object. Initialize a CUserModeHangReport object. Create the actual report by calling CHangReport::Create() . Submit the error report by calling CHangReport::Submit() . Obviously, this is an oversimplification, since a lot is happening , but the details are not very relevant for this blog post. SnapshotCaptureMain This mode, triggered by -pss , requires the same arguments as UserCrashMainSEH . -ip the initiating process id. -p the process id. -s a handle to a shared memory object. Note that here we’re dealing with a handle to the shared memory, opposed to a global name. The flow for this function is straightforward. Validate input. Open a handle to specified process ( -p ). Open a handle to specified initiating process( -ip ). If there is none, open a handle to same process as specified with -p . Make a snapshot of that process. The last step — creating a snapshot — is actually an interesting procedure, as it might offer some opportunities for LSASS dumping again. This does require some tinkering, as WerFault performs certain checks on the validity of the data in the shared memory section. Also it validates some other settings. For example, if the taking snapshots is allowed on the current system. The one thing which is still unclear to me, is how WerFault is supposed to MapViewOfFile , where the handle is directly a command-line argument and thus — by definition — external to WerFault. This is almost certainly related to shared memory sections, and the error reporting port which all Windows processes seem to have. SilentProcessExitMain This function is implemented as a proxy to the function WerUIReportSilentProcessExit in werui.dll . See the screenshow below. The implementation of SilentProcessExitMain in werfault.exe. Jumping into the implementation of this function in werui.dll , we see more weird things happening. It parses argc/argv looking for the following command-line arguments: -i The initiating process id. If the process is self-terminating, this is the same as the exiting process. If the silent process termination is triggered cross-process, this is the id of the process that started the termination. -e The exiting process. -t The thread id that sends the SilentProcessExit signal to WerFault. This is a thread id inside the process referenced by -i . -c The statuscode passed to ExitThread/TerminateThread. The table describing the registry entries “accidentily” documents this as well. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/debugger/registry-entries-for-silent-process-exit#monitor-process Since the details of how “Silent Process Exit” works are described in a lot of detail and the reversing didn’t reveal anything new, we won’t go into any more depth on this. KernelCrashMain KernelCrashMain handles both crash dumps and live kernel reports, so the name is a little misleading. It first parses the argument after -k to select an operation for this mode. The command-line options which determine the operation are: -c “Convert dump and report”. This operation processes an existing crash dump, queues the resulting kernel report and then attempts to report from the kernel queue. -q “Report from KQueue”. This operation skips the dump processing and starts working on reporting from the kernel queue directly. -l “Report live report”. Find and queue one live report into the KQueue. -lc “Convert live dump and report”. Process a full live dump and then submit it to WER. -lcq “Report all live reports”. This traverses the KQueue and submits each item to WER. Final remarks WerFault.exe is more than just a crash reporting utility. Depending on its command-line arguments, it can perform a variety of operations, including creating process snapshots, cloning processes, and generating memory dumps. Hopefully, this breakdown helps demystify some of WerFault’s less-documented behavior and provides a useful reference for analysts trying to distinguish legitimate activity from potential abuse. Dissecting WerFault

Henri Hambartsumyan

This blog post documents the command-line parameters of WerFault.exe, obtained by reverse engineering the binary. Some inner WerFault workings are also discussed.

A side note: I started this small side project in 2023. Reversing was, back then, still mostly a manual effort. Current AI tools can do this in a few minutes with probably more accurate descriptions, but I hope you can enjoy some artisanal reverse engineering.

Introduction

Modern Windows versions come with a large number of executables files. My system32 folder alone currently has 879 .exe files, while the wider C:\Windows has 5748 .exe files. However, only a small selection of those binaries have properties which are special and worth investigating. 

One of those binaries is WerFault.exe and its significant other WerFaultSecure.exe. There are two main reasons why WerFault is interesting from security perspective:

  • It’s designed to create memory dumps and snapshots of other processes.
  • There is limited documentation on the inner workings and command-line arguments.

The first reason is interesting from an offensive perspective. Attackers can and do leverage WerFault. For example, to dump LSASS with “silentprocessexit”. But are there any other attack paths to leverage for offensive purposes?

The second reason — limited documentation — is very annoying for detection engineering, incident triage and incident response purposes. I found a blog post from Helge Klein, which documents some things. Also, Hexacorn has a blog post on this topic, but in there are still unknowns which intrigue me. The best documentation I found so far was (of course 😉) the Windows Internals book. 

In this blog post, I’ll combine the information from the aforementioned three sources with knowledge obtained by reversing WerFault. 

Dispatching the call

A logical place to start understanding the command-line argument is to start with the wmain function. Loading werfault.exe into IDA and loading the Microsoft-provided symbols, we can hit the ground running.

Very quickly inside wmain you can see the parsing of the command-line arguments.

 

 Parsing the command-line arguments in wmain.

And thanks to the symbols provided by Microsoft, we can already make out that the the first command-line option determines the “mode” of WerFault.

Here, we notice a few things:

  • The wmain function is a dispatcher. Based on the first command-line argument, it calls the corresponding “main” function.
  • All the arguments are with a - except /hc and /h.
  • Both /hc and /h do the same. 

All other command-line arguments are dependent on the specific function. The specific features, as suggested by the functions names, are also confirmed by the two blog posts mentioned earlier and the Windows Internals book. So far, so good.

In the next sections, we’ll explore each of these functionalities individually.

UserCrashMainSEH

Based on the name, we can fairly assume that this function is invoked whenever a normal “user process” crashes. SEH in this context likely points to Structured Exception Handling.

Looking again, the code is fairly easy to read in disassembled form, as well as in assembly. 

Here, we’re seeing again the parsing of the command-line arguments passed to UserCrashMain. Based on the error messages we can drive:

  • -s refers to a shared memory handle.
  • -p refers to the process id of the crashing process.
  • -ip refers to a initiating process id.

 The relevant steps performed by this function:

  1. Parse and validate command-line arguments. -s is mandatory and -p are mandatory. -ip is optional.
  2. Open a handle to the process with pid -p.
  3. If -ipis set, open a handle to the process with pid -ip.
  4. Else open a new handle to the process with pid -p and use it as if it’s the initiation process id. 
  5. Call WerpInitiateCrashReporting — as seen in screenshot below.

A few things to note in this screenshot:

  • XerDumpNotifyStart and XerDumpNotifyComplete are both imported from ext-ms-win-wer-xbox-l1-1-1.dll. This is a weird library I can’t find on any system I have access to. I’m also unsure what the relationship is with xbox. If you have any clue or have a copy of this binary, please let me know. Google only has 3 hits on this filename. There is nothing on VT.
  • WerpInitiateCrashReporting is imported from faultrep.dll.

There is plenty of things going on inside WerpInitiateCrashReporting, but we’ll skip that for now as it’s not relevant for the scope of this blog post.

ReflectionServerMain

This next function name doesn’t reveal much (to me) about what it does. Looking at the code, we see that this function only accepts one command-line argument with its corresponding value, being -pr XXXX. If the number of parameters provided is incorrect, it returns error code 0x80070057, which translates to “The parameter is incorrect”.

In the happy flow, we’re going to start the ReflectedDumpServer, passing in the value of the -pr argument — whatever that means.

The value of the -pr is “The name of the file mapping object to be opened.” It’s passed to the lpName parameter of OpenFileMappingW. Based on the description of the workflow in the Windows Internals book Chapter 10, section “Windows Error Reporting”, I suspect the handle name passed to WerFault is the name of the shared memory object, potentially created by the crashing process. More debugging and reversing is required to confirm this. 

While following the decompiled code in IDA, it seems like the main goal of this mode ends up in a call to RtlCreateProcessReflection. This seems to be an undocumented function. However, there are plenty of details documented by all kinds of security researchers. Moreover, some details are described in “Windows Internals, 6th edition, Part 2”. The latest edition (7th) doesn’t include this section. It’s a function which allows a process to be cloned. The function creates a minidump with MiniDumpWriteDump , clones the process and “resumes” it. I suspect this is an attempt to restore a crashing process. But again, it requires more reversing to properly understand this.

This is potentially a vector to either create a memory dump of LSASS directly or to clone LSASS with RtlCreateProcessReflection and then dump it. But this full attack chain is still unproven.

WerCoreReportingHang

Before diving into how this function works, note that in multiple ways this functionality feels like it’s been bolted on “after the fact”. First, there is the obvious difference in expecting command-line arguments with a / instead of a -. Next is the fact that it accepts two different command-line switches for the same function. All others have exactly one switch. Finally, the way the function is invoked is different. Consider the next screenshot from IDA.

All functions take the full argc/argv pair, as passed to wmain , while a call to WerCoreReportHang strips the first command-line argument from argc/argv. 

The only command-line arguments which seems to be actually parsed in this function is the /SHARED argument. While based on actual process creation data in various environments, the /t and /p arguments seem to be passed. Either way, /p most likely refers to the process id again, while /t might refer to a thread id in case of a thread hang, but I can’t confirm this based on the code.

As the function name suggest, this function is meant for error reporting on processes that are hanging. The first step is to check if the system has been configured to attach a debugger, based on HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\Hangs\Debugger. If a debugger is set, it executes the debugger. If applicable, it then waits until a debugger is attached and breaks. 

Next, it resets the PATH environment variable to the System32 folder, and sets a bunch more environment variables starting with _NT_. 

Then, it checks if a /SHARED argument is provided, which points to a shared memory object, just like earlier. If so, this shared memory is opened, copied locally and the structure is validated to see if it matches the undocumented type SharedHangRepData struct. 

We’ll skip most of the details of the next steps, but roughly the following happens:

  1. Initialize a CProcessInformation object containing the process id of the crashing process.
  2. Initialize a CHangReport object.
  3. Initialize a CUserModeHangReport object.
  4. Create the actual report by calling CHangReport::Create().
  5. Submit the error report by calling CHangReport::Submit().

Obviously, this is an oversimplification, since a lot is happening , but the details are not very relevant for this blog post. 

SnapshotCaptureMain

This mode, triggered by -pss, requires the same arguments as UserCrashMainSEH.

  • -ip the initiating process id.
  • -p the process id.
  • -s a handle to a shared memory object.

Note that here we’re dealing with a handle to the shared memory, opposed to a global name.

The flow for this function is straightforward.

  1. Validate input.
  2. Open a handle to specified process (-p).
  3. Open a handle to specified initiating process(-ip). If there is none, open a handle to same process as specified with -p.
  4. Make a snapshot of that process.

The last step — creating a snapshot — is actually an interesting procedure, as it might offer some opportunities for LSASS dumping again. This does require some tinkering, as WerFault performs certain checks on the validity of the data in the shared memory section. Also it validates some other settings. For example, if the taking snapshots is allowed on the current system.

The one thing which is still unclear to me, is how WerFault is supposed to MapViewOfFile , where the handle is directly a command-line argument and thus — by definition — external to WerFault. This is almost certainly related to shared memory sections, and the error reporting port which all Windows processes seem to have.

SilentProcessExitMain

This function is implemented as a proxy to the function WerUIReportSilentProcessExit in werui.dll. See the screenshow below.

The implementation of SilentProcessExitMain in werfault.exe.

Jumping into the implementation of this function in werui.dll, we see more weird things happening. It parses argc/argv looking for the following command-line arguments:

  • -i The initiating process id. If the process is self-terminating, this is the same as the exiting process. If the silent process termination is triggered cross-process, this is the id of the process that started the termination.
  • -e The exiting process. 
  • -t The thread id that sends the SilentProcessExit signal to WerFault. This is a thread id inside the process referenced by -i.
  • -c The statuscode passed to ExitThread/TerminateThread.

The table describing the registry entries “accidentily” documents this as well. 

Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/debugger/registry-entries-for-silent-process-exit#monitor-process

Since the details of how “Silent Process Exit” works are described in a lot of detail and the reversing didn’t reveal anything new, we won’t go into any more depth on this. 

KernelCrashMain

KernelCrashMain handles both crash dumps and live kernel reports, so the name is a little misleading. It first parses the argument after -k to select an operation for this mode.

The command-line options which determine the operation are:

  • -c “Convert dump and report”. This operation processes an existing crash dump, queues the resulting kernel report and then attempts to report from the kernel queue.
  • -q “Report from KQueue”. This operation skips the dump processing and starts working on reporting from the kernel queue directly.
  • -l “Report live report”. Find and queue one live report into the KQueue.
  • -lc “Convert live dump and report”. Process a full live dump and then submit it to WER.
  • -lcq “Report all live reports”. This traverses the KQueue and submits each item to WER.

Final remarks

WerFault.exe is more than just a crash reporting utility. Depending on its command-line arguments, it can perform a variety of operations, including creating process snapshots, cloning processes, and generating memory dumps.

Hopefully, this breakdown helps demystify some of WerFault’s less-documented behavior and provides a useful reference for analysts trying to distinguish legitimate activity from potential abuse.

items.title: How to Export FortiSIEM Logs
items.summary: Use FortiSIEM’s REST event query API. Post an XML query to /phoenix/rest/query/eventQuery, which returns a query ID, poll the progress until it reaches 100, then fetch the events. The results come back as XML. The original log line of each event is in the rawEventMsg attribute, so a few lines of Python turn the result into raw logs. Exports from the Analytics screen come out in formats LogTotal doesn’t read today. FortiSIEM is common wherever Fortinet runs the network, and it often holds far more than firewall logs. Prime Core has 19,692 detection rules for FortiSIEM, mapped to 664 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get events out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An API user. Use an account with rights to run analytics queries. The API authenticates with basic auth, with the organization in the username: super/ on an enterprise install, / for a specific organization in a service provider install. Retention. Online event storage is limited. Older events may sit in archive storage that needs extra steps. Attribute names. FortiSIEM queries use its own attribute names, such as reptDevName (reporting device), reptDevIpAddr, eventType and phRecvTime. Build the filter in Analytics first. Export with the event query API Save the query as query.xml: LogTotal export phRecvTime,reptDevIpAddr,eventType,rawEventMsg 1792368000 1792454400 reptDevName = "web-03" The interval is epoch seconds for 2026-10-19 00:00 UTC to 2026-10-20 00:00 UTC. Then run it: FSM="https://fortisiem.example.com" AUTH="super/apiuser:$FSM_PASS" QID=$(curl -sS -u "$AUTH" -X POST -H 'Content-Type: text/xml' --data @query.xml "$FSM/phoenix/rest/query/eventQuery") until [ "$(curl -sS -u "$AUTH" "$FSM/phoenix/rest/query/progress/$QID")" = "100" ]; do sleep 5; done curl -sS -u "$AUTH" "$FSM/phoenix/rest/query/events/$QID/0/1000" > fsm_web03_1019.xml The last two path segments are the start offset and the count. Page through large results in steps of 1,000. Then pull out the raw messages: import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET root = ET.parse("fsm_web03_1019.xml").getroot() with open("fsm_web03_1019.log", "w") as out: for attr in root.iter("attribute"): if attr.get("name") == "rawEventMsg" and attr.text: out.write(attr.text.strip() + "\n") Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. What this looks like on real data. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 401 Organization missing from the username Use super/ or / Query returns an error instead of an ID XML syntax or an unknown attribute name Test the filter in Analytics; check attribute names Progress never reaches 100 Query too broad Narrow the time range and filter rawEventMsg empty The attribute wasn’t selected Add rawEventMsg to AttrList Old events missing They’re in archive storage Check archive options FAQ Why XML? That’s what this FortiSIEM API speaks. The Python step converts it to the original raw lines, which is usually what you want to upload anyway. Can I export incidents instead? Incidents have their own API calls. For LogTotal, export the events behind them.
items.summary_html:
Use FortiSIEM’s REST event query API. Post an XML query to /phoenix/rest/query/eventQuery, which returns a query ID, poll the progress until it reaches 100, then fetch the events. The results come back as XML. The original log line of each event is in the rawEventMsg attribute, so a few lines of Python turn the result into raw logs. Exports from the Analytics screen come out in formats LogTotal doesn’t read today. 

FortiSIEM is common wherever Fortinet runs the network, and it often holds far more than firewall logs. Prime Core has 19,692 detection rules for FortiSIEM, mapped to 664 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get events out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

An API user. Use an account with rights to run analytics queries. The API authenticates with basic auth, with the organization in the username: super/ on an enterprise install, / for a specific organization in a service provider install.

Retention. Online event storage is limited. Older events may sit in archive storage that needs extra steps. 

Attribute names. FortiSIEM queries use its own attribute names, such as reptDevName (reporting device), reptDevIpAddr, eventType and phRecvTime. Build the filter in Analytics first.

Export with the event query API

Save the query as query.xml:


LogTotal export
  phRecvTime,reptDevIpAddr,eventType,rawEventMsg
  17923680001792454400
  
    reptDevName = "web-03"
 

The interval is epoch seconds for 2026-10-19 00:00 UTC to 2026-10-20 00:00 UTC. Then run it:

FSM="https://fortisiem.example.com"
AUTH="super/apiuser:$FSM_PASS"

QID=$(curl -sS -u "$AUTH" -X POST -H 'Content-Type: text/xml' --data @query.xml "$FSM/phoenix/rest/query/eventQuery")
until [ "$(curl -sS -u "$AUTH" "$FSM/phoenix/rest/query/progress/$QID")" = "100" ]; do sleep 5; done
curl -sS -u "$AUTH" "$FSM/phoenix/rest/query/events/$QID/0/1000" > fsm_web03_1019.xml

The last two path segments are the start offset and the count. Page through large results in steps of 1,000. Then pull out the raw messages:

import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

root = ET.parse("fsm_web03_1019.xml").getroot()
with open("fsm_web03_1019.log", "w") as out:
    for attr in root.iter("attribute"):
        if attr.get("name") == "rawEventMsg" and attr.text:
            out.write(attr.text.strip() + "\n")
Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file.
  2. Sanitize.
  3. Review.

What this looks like on real data. 

When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFix401Organization missing from the usernameUse super/ or /Query returns an error instead of an IDXML syntax or an unknown attribute nameTest the filter in Analytics; check attribute namesProgress never reaches 100Query too broadNarrow the time range and filterrawEventMsg emptyThe attribute wasn’t selectedAdd rawEventMsg to AttrListOld events missingThey’re in archive storageCheck archive options
FAQ

Why XML?

That’s what this FortiSIEM API speaks. The Python step converts it to the original raw lines, which is usually what you want to upload anyway.

Can I export incidents instead?

Incidents have their own API calls. For LogTotal, export the events behind them.

items.title: How to Export Graylog Logs
items.summary: Graylog keeps its messages in OpenSearch or Elasticsearch, so you have two routes. Use the Graylog REST API, authenticated with an access token, or query the backend indices (graylog_* by default) directly with a script. Either way you get JSON. The original line is in message, and in full_message for some inputs. The export in the Graylog web interface produces a format LogTotal doesn’t read today. Graylog is a popular open log management platform, often the first central logging a team sets up. Prime Core has 23,274 detection rules for Graylog, mapped to 671 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get messages out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An access token. In Graylog, open your user’s settings and create a token. With the API, you authenticate as :token: the token as the username and the word token as the password. Backend access, if you go direct. The OpenSearch or Elasticsearch cluster behind Graylog often isn’t reachable from outside. Ask whoever runs it for a read-only account. Streams and index sets. Graylog routes messages into streams, and streams map to index sets with their own prefixes and retention. Know which index set holds your data. Option 1: Graylog REST API GL="https://graylog.example.com" curl -sS -u "$GL_TOKEN:token" -H 'Accept: application/json' -G "$GL/api/search/universal/absolute" \ --data-urlencode 'query=source:web-03' \ --data-urlencode 'from=2026-10-19T00:00:00.000Z' \ --data-urlencode 'to=2026-10-20T00:00:00.000Z' \ --data-urlencode 'limit=10000' \ | jq -c '.messages[].message' > graylog_web03_1019.jsonl Newer Graylog versions favor the Views search API. For large exports, Option 2 is more reliable. Option 2: Query the backend indices This is the same approach as our pointed at Graylog’s indices: import json, os from opensearchpy import OpenSearch, helpers client = OpenSearch("https://opensearch.example.com:9200", http_auth=("reader", os.environ["OS_PASSWORD"]), verify_certs=True) query = {"query": {"bool": {"filter": [ {"term": {"source": "web-03"}}, {"range": {"timestamp": {"gte": "2026-10-19 00:00:00.000", "lt": "2026-10-20 00:00:00.000"}}}, ]}}} with open("graylog_web03_1019.jsonl", "w") as out: for hit in helpers.scan(client, index="graylog_*", query=query, size=1000): out.write(json.dumps(hit["_source"]) + "\n") Graylog stores timestamp as yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS in UTC, which is why the range uses that format. For a backend running Elasticsearch, use the elasticsearch client the same way. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 401 from the API Token auth written wrong Use :token 404 on the search endpoint Endpoint not available in your version Use Option 2, or the Views API Backend query returns nothing Wrong index prefix, or the timestamp format Check index sets; use yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS Backend not reachable Cluster not exposed Ask for read-only access, or use the API FAQ Message or full_message? Message is always there. full_message appears for some inputs, such as GELF, and can hold more detail. Export both if you have them. Does this work for Graylog Cloud? The API route does. Direct backend access usually isn’t available on hosted plans.
items.summary_html:
Graylog keeps its messages in OpenSearch or Elasticsearch, so you have two routes. Use the Graylog REST API, authenticated with an access token, or query the backend indices (graylog_* by default) directly with a script. Either way you get JSON. The original line is in message, and in full_message for some inputs. The export in the Graylog web interface produces a format LogTotal doesn’t read today. 

Graylog is a popular open log management platform, often the first central logging a team sets up. Prime Core has 23,274 detection rules for Graylog, mapped to 671 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get messages out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

An access token. In Graylog, open your user’s settings and create a token. With the API, you authenticate as :token: the token as the username and the word token as the password.

Backend access, if you go direct. The OpenSearch or Elasticsearch cluster behind Graylog often isn’t reachable from outside. Ask whoever runs it for a read-only account.

Streams and index sets. Graylog routes messages into streams, and streams map to index sets with their own prefixes and retention. Know which index set holds your data.

Option 1: Graylog REST API 
GL="https://graylog.example.com"

curl -sS -u "$GL_TOKEN:token" -H 'Accept: application/json' -G "$GL/api/search/universal/absolute" \
  --data-urlencode 'query=source:web-03' \
  --data-urlencode 'from=2026-10-19T00:00:00.000Z' \
  --data-urlencode 'to=2026-10-20T00:00:00.000Z' \
  --data-urlencode 'limit=10000' \
  | jq -c '.messages[].message' > graylog_web03_1019.jsonl

Newer Graylog versions favor the Views search API. For large exports, Option 2 is more reliable.

Option 2: Query the backend indices

This is the same approach as our pointed at Graylog’s indices:

import json, os
from opensearchpy import OpenSearch, helpers

client = OpenSearch("https://opensearch.example.com:9200",
                    http_auth=("reader", os.environ["OS_PASSWORD"]), verify_certs=True)
query = {"query": {"bool": {"filter": [
    {"term": {"source": "web-03"}},
    {"range": {"timestamp": {"gte": "2026-10-19 00:00:00.000", "lt": "2026-10-20 00:00:00.000"}}},
]}}}

with open("graylog_web03_1019.jsonl", "w") as out:
    for hit in helpers.scan(client, index="graylog_*", query=query, size=1000):
        out.write(json.dumps(hit["_source"]) + "\n")

Graylog stores timestamp as yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS in UTC, which is why the range uses that format. For a backend running Elasticsearch, use the elasticsearch client the same way.

Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. 
  2. Sanitize. 
  3. Review. 
When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFix401 from the APIToken auth written wrongUse :token404 on the search endpointEndpoint not available in your versionUse Option 2, or the Views APIBackend query returns nothingWrong index prefix, or the timestamp formatCheck index sets; use yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSSBackend not reachableCluster not exposedAsk for read-only access, or use the API
FAQ

Message or full_message?

Message is always there. full_message appears for some inputs, such as GELF, and can hold more detail. Export both if you have them.

Does this work for Graylog Cloud?

The API route does. Direct backend access usually isn’t available on hosted plans.

items.title: How to Export Wazuh Logs
items.summary: Wazuh keeps its data in two places. On the Wazuh manager, alerts are written to /var/ossec/logs/alerts/alerts.json, one JSON object per line, and rotated daily into compressed files by date. The same alerts are indexed in the Wazuh indexer (OpenSearch), in wazuh-alerts-4.x-*. Either way, the original log line that triggered an alert is in full_log. To export every event, not just the ones that matched a rule, the manager needs archiving turned on. Wazuh is the most widely used open-source SIEM and XDR, and its data is easy to get at once you know where to look. Prime Core has 23,542 detection rules for Wazuh, mapped to 671 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to export alerts and events, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. items.title: Frida 17.26.1 Released
items.summary: A quick one with a single QuickJS fix from @mrmacete . Since the rebase onto current QuickJS, the runtime marks “no exception pending” with an uninitialized value rather than null . Three spots in our own patches still reset the pending exception to null after temporarily stashing it: when suspending the runtime so another thread can use it, while running Error.prepareStackTrace() , and while calling the hook that provides lazily created globals. Current QuickJS reads that null as an exception still pending, with null as its value. Francesco found it and fixed all three. Thanks! Enjoy! Changelog quickjs: Use the uninitialized value as the no-exception sentinel when suspending the runtime, preparing stack traces, and resolving globals through the access hook. Thanks @mrmacete !
