items.title: Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Find GitHub Secrets and Steal Azure Key Vault Data in Just 5 Minutes
items.summary: Hackers are using the ARTEX AI framework to find exposed credentials on GitHub and turn them into access to cloud systems. In one observed case, an AI agent moved from searching public repositories for application secrets to stealing data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes, showing how quickly a coding mistake can become a cloud security incident. The operation combines credential hunting, automated analysis, and follow-on attacks with less hands-on work from human operators. Instead of simply collecting leaked keys, the agents investigate what those keys can access and pursue valuable resources. The five-minute finding describes one documented case, not the time required for every attack involving the framework. Microsoft Threat Intelligence and Microsoft Security Research identified the malicious activity in a November 5 report, tracing GitHub scanning to August 2026. Researchers described ARTEX as an offensive AI framework, rather than a conventional malware family. Earlier reporting on ARTEX enterprise attack automation explains how agents interpret results and select subsequent actions, helping attackers connect familiar weaknesses faster. Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Find GitHub Secrets The agents submitted large volumes of GitHub searches combining target organization names with terms associated with secrets, cloud platforms, and AI providers. Exposed material included application credentials and API keys for AI inference services. These searches target authentication data accidentally committed in scripts, configuration files, or other source code. Once useful credentials were found, agents obtained tokens for compromised OAuth applications and used their permissions to explore cloud resources. Microsoft observed agents extracting Azure Key Vault secrets and searching Azure DevOps for additional credentials. The wider problem of active GitHub credential exposure helps explain why this approach remains effective: publicly disclosed secrets can remain usable until their owners revoke or rotate them. In follow-on activity beginning as early as October 28, attackers used valid application credentials to access Microsoft Entra ID tenants and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. Service principals, the identities applications use to authenticate, enabled access to dozens of applications across multiple tenants. Some compromised credentials belonged to vendor-owned multitenant applications, extending the risk to downstream customers. The attackers mapped subscriptions, permissions, resource groups, and AI deployments. They targeted storage keys, connection strings, App Service settings, publishing credentials, and Azure Kubernetes Service credentials. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) observed across the credential abuse attack chain (Source – Microsoft) Compromised applications also accessed SharePoint and OneDrive, with observed file downloads and mailbox-item access. Agents additionally used Azure VM Run Command, a legitimate feature that can execute scripts inside virtual machines. The activity showed adaptive troubleshooting. After failed requests mixed Key Vault data-plane API versions with Azure Resource Manager control-plane endpoints, the agent retried approximately 28 seconds later using ARM version 2023-07-01 and received successful responses. Similar corrections followed failed Azure SQL and Application Insights requests. Such behavior supports the broader concern around autonomous AI credential theft , where automation can reduce delays between discovery and misuse. Detecting and Containing AI-Driven Cloud Credential Abuse Microsoft recommends treating publicly exposed credentials as compromised, even after developers delete the original code. Responders should revoke or rotate affected secrets, investigate historical use, and replace credentials stored in any Key Vault the compromised application could read. Disabling affected service principals may be necessary; already-issued tokens remain valid until expiry. Detection should connect identity events with subsequent cloud operations. Security teams should review Entra service-principal sign-ins, Azure Activity records, Key Vault diagnostics, storage logs, and Microsoft 365 audit data. One address accessing several service principals, or one application rapidly requesting tokens across ARM, Key Vault, Storage, and Graph, warrants investigation. IP matches alone should not determine attribution. Longer-term protection means reducing reliance on long-lived secrets through managed identities, enforcing least privilege, and enabling GitHub secret scanning and push protection. Microsoft also recommends monitoring secondary public repositories for leaked organizational credentials. Behavioral detections remain essential because attackers can change source addresses and user-agent strings, while legitimate tools can produce traffic resembling individual attack steps. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator Type Source-reported context 199.19.77[.]84 IPv4 Successful application sign-ins; cloud discovery and credential abuse. 199.19.77[.]18 IPv4 Sign-in source; Tor exit node potentially carrying unrelated activity. 65.87.223[.]26 IPv4 Potentially associated malicious operations; App Service token attempts. 157.22.126[.]128 IPv4 Separately observed reconnaissance targeting victims’ Azure AI workloads. Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: CVE-2026-123158: OpenSSH Password Authentication Bypass Affects Alpine Linux
items.summary: A high-severity vulnerability in OpenSSH can allow unauthenticated remote attackers to bypass password authentication on certain Linux systems by submitting an overlong password. Tracked as CVE-2026-123158 and dubbed SSHhole, the flaw carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 and primarily impacts Linux environments where sshd is linked against musl libc and operates without PAM. Alpine Linux is the most prominent affected platform because its standard openssh-server package uses this configuration by default. The vulnerability results from an unexpected interaction between OpenSSH password validation and musl libc’s crypt() implementation. When an excessively long password is supplied, crypt() can return the string * to indicate an error. Some Linux accounts that are configured without a conventional password also store * in the password field of /etc/shadow. Under vulnerable conditions, sshd can incorrectly interpret the matching values as successful authentication. An attacker does not need to know the target user’s password. If an exposed SSH service meets the required conditions, an attacker who can reach the service can authenticate to certain accounts using a password in the vulnerable length range. The impact depends on the privileges assigned to the compromised account. Access to a privileged service account or an account capable of using doas or another privilege escalation mechanism could lead to full system compromise. Contact Sales OpenSSH addressed the issue in Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2, released on November 5, 2026. Alpine Linux simultaneously released patched OpenSSH packages for all supported branches and several older branches. The OpenSSH team describes the release as containing a critical security workaround for Linux systems using musl libc with PAM disabled. Public reproduction environments and proof-of-concept material are already available. However, as of November 6, 2026, the reviewed sources do not report confirmed exploitation of the vulnerability in real-world attacks, and the flaw has not been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Organizations can strengthen defenses against emerging authentication bypass vulnerabilities with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, accelerating threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Security teams can also use Prime Architect to transform vulnerability intelligence into hunting queries and detection logic tailored to their available SSH, authentication, endpoint, and network telemetry. Detect CVE-2026-123158 by monitoring successful password-based SSH logins to accounts that normally use key-only authentication, unusual authentication attempts containing abnormally long passwords, unexpected remote access to service accounts, and post-authentication activity inconsistent with the account’s normal behavior. Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. CVE-2026-123158 analysis CVE-2026-123158 affects OpenSSH sshd before Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 when it runs on Linux with musl libc and password authentication occurs without PAM. The CVE carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 with the vector AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H, reflecting remote exploitation without prior privileges or user interaction but requiring a specific system and account configuration. The root cause lies in the interaction between OpenSSH and the password hashing function provided by musl libc. On systems where PAM is disabled, sshd performs password validation using the system’s crypt() functionality. For a typical account, /etc/shadow contains a cryptographic password hash, and the value generated from the user’s submitted password is compared against that stored hash. musl libc behaves differently when the supplied password exceeds its supported input length. For passwords longer than 256 bytes, crypt() returns * as an error value rather than a normal password hash. The problem arises because * is also commonly used in /etc/shadow for accounts that do not have a traditional password configured. If a vulnerable sshd receives an overlong password for one of these accounts, the authentication flow can effectively compare the * returned by crypt() with the * stored in the account’s shadow entry. The values match, and authentication can incorrectly succeed. The CVE description states that, for affected account configurations, passwords between 256 and 1024 characters can result in successful authentication. Independent reproductions describe passwords exceeding the normal 256-byte boundary as sufficient to trigger the vulnerable condition. The flaw is therefore not a universal password bypass affecting every OpenSSH deployment. Several specific conditions must align. First, the server must use musl libc. Alpine Linux is the primary mainstream example, although other embedded or minimal Linux environments can also use musl. Second, sshd must authenticate users without PAM. Alpine’s standard openssh-server package is built without PAM, while the alternative openssh-server-pam configuration is protected when UsePAM yes is enabled. Third, password authentication must be enabled. PasswordAuthentication yes is the relevant configuration. Systems configured for public-key-only authentication with PasswordAuthentication no are not exposed to the documented attack path. Finally, the attacker needs an account whose password field contains *. These can include key-only users, accounts created without passwords, some identities provided through directory services, and certain cloud-image users. Alpine also notes an additional condition: at least one local account must contain a $5$ or $6$-style password hash for the vulnerable authentication path to operate as described. The root account deserves special attention. Alpine commonly stores root:*, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password prevents password authentication directly to root. As a result, a standard Alpine installation does not automatically expose direct root login through this bug. That protection does not eliminate the broader risk. If another account with * in its password field is remotely accessible and has administrative rights through doas, sudo, container capabilities, or other privileged mechanisms, successful authentication can still provide a path to complete system compromise. Alpine’s official tiny-cloud images are particularly relevant. Security research identified versions where the alpine account could meet the vulnerable conditions and was also able to use doas to gain elevated privileges. This illustrates why defenders should evaluate account privileges rather than assuming the vulnerability provides either harmless user access or automatic root access in every environment. glibc-based Linux distributions such as Debian, Ubuntu, and RHEL are not affected by this specific vulnerability because the vulnerable behavior depends on musl libc’s password hashing implementation. Systems using PAM for SSH password validation are likewise outside the documented vulnerable configuration. Containers require similar qualification. Alpine is widely used as a container base image, but ordinary containers that do not run sshd are not vulnerable through this attack path. The primary concern is containers, appliances, development environments, or legacy workloads that explicitly install and expose an SSH server. The CVE-2026-123158 PoC landscape has developed quickly. Public reproduction labs are referenced directly by the vulnerability record, demonstrating that defenders should assume the authentication bypass can be reproduced without access to private exploit research. This materially raises remediation urgency even though confirmed malicious exploitation has not yet been reported. The vulnerability was reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. OpenSSH publicly released version 10.6p2 with the security workaround on November 5, 2026. The reviewed primary sources do not specify the exact date on which the researcher initially discovered or privately reported the issue. The OpenSSH fix adds validation designed to prevent error values and invalid short password hashes from being accepted during password authentication. OpenSSH notes that it considers the underlying root cause to exist outside sshd, but because the condition can be exploited through the SSH server, the project implemented a defensive workaround in OpenSSH itself. Alpine Linux has backported the correction across multiple branches: Alpine branch Fixed OpenSSH package edge 10.6_p2-r0 3.24 10.3_p1-r2 3.23 10.2_p1-r1 3.22 10.0_p1-r11 3.21 9.9_p2-r1 3.20 9.7_p1-r6 3.19 9.6_p1-r3 3.18 9.3_p2-r4 3.17 9.1_p1-r7 3.16 9.0_p1-r6 Administrators should rely on their distribution package status rather than the SSH version banner alone. Linux distributions frequently backport security patches without changing the upstream OpenSSH version displayed during the SSH handshake. A server displaying an older version string may therefore already contain the vendor fix. For CVE-2026-123158 detection, defenders should prioritize SSH authentication telemetry. A particularly strong hunting signal is a successful password login to an account that is intended to use only public-key authentication or that has no usable password configured. On Alpine systems, administrators can review /var/log/messages, centralized authentication logs, SIEM records, or equivalent telemetry for Accepted password events involving unexpected service, key-only, or administrative accounts. Defenders should correlate successful authentication with source IP addresses, login times, session duration, commands executed after login, privilege elevation, changes to authorized_keys, account creation, scheduled jobs, and unexpected outbound network connections. Network telemetry can also help identify exposed systems. Externally reachable SSH services advertising password or keyboard-interactive authentication should receive higher remediation priority, particularly when the underlying system is Alpine or another musl-based distribution. At present, there are no campaign-specific CVE-2026-123158 IOCs such as confirmed attacker IP addresses, domains, malware hashes, or command-and-control infrastructure. The absence of static indicators makes behavioral monitoring of SSH authentication and subsequent session activity particularly important. CVE-2026-123158 Mitigation The primary remediation is to install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the corrected package supplied by the Linux distribution. Alpine administrators should update the full system using the current package repositories and restart sshd afterward. Updating the package alone does not replace the already running SSH daemon process. Organizations running Alpine-based containers should rebuild and redeploy any image that installs openssh-server. Simply updating the host operating system does not patch vulnerable OpenSSH packages embedded inside container images. Administrators should also identify exposure before assuming that every Alpine host is vulnerable. Key checks include: Determine whether the host uses musl libc. Verify whether sshd is running with PAM disabled. Check whether password authentication is enabled. Identify login-capable accounts whose /etc/shadow password field is *. Review the privileges assigned to those accounts. Confirm the installed OpenSSH package against the distribution’s corrected package version. If immediate patching is impossible, organizations should disable SSH password authentication. Configure: PasswordAuthentication no and, where applicable: KbdInteractiveAuthentication no Administrators should confirm that public-key authentication works before applying this configuration to avoid losing legitimate administrative access. The SSH configuration should then be validated and the daemon reloaded or restarted. Afterward, external verification should confirm that the server offers only public-key authentication. Restricting network accessibility provides additional defense in depth. SSH should generally be reachable only from trusted administrative networks, VPN infrastructure, bastion hosts, or explicit source-IP allowlists rather than being universally exposed to the internet. Organizations should also reconsider whether SSH is required inside containers at all. Modern orchestration environments usually provide alternatives such as docker exec or kubectl exec, eliminating an unnecessary remotely reachable authentication service. For potentially exposed systems, review historical successful password logins occurring before remediation. Pay particular attention to accounts configured without passwords and identities normally expected to authenticate exclusively with SSH keys. If an unexpected successful login is identified, treat the account as potentially compromised. Review shell history where available, process execution, privilege escalation, new or modified authorized_keys entries, user and group changes, cron jobs, startup scripts, package installation, and outbound network connections. Credentials and keys accessible to the compromised account should be considered potentially exposed and rotated according to the findings of the investigation. If the account had administrative privileges, defenders should expand the investigation to the entire host and any systems reachable using credentials stored there. Public proof-of-concept material means organizations should not wait for evidence of widespread attacks before applying the fix. The exploitation prerequisites narrow the vulnerable population, but systems that meet those conditions can be accessed remotely without knowledge of a valid password. FAQ What is CVE-2026-123158 and how does it work? CVE-2026-123158 is a password authentication bypass affecting OpenSSH sshd on Linux systems using musl libc without PAM. When an excessively long password is passed to musl’s crypt() function, it can return * as an error value. If the target account also has * stored in /etc/shadow, vulnerable sshd configurations can incorrectly treat the values as matching and allow authentication. When was CVE-2026-123158 first discovered? The vulnerability was reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. OpenSSH published the security fix in Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 on November 5, 2026, and the CVE became public the same day. The currently reviewed primary advisories do not disclose the exact date of the researcher’s original private discovery. What is the impact of CVE-2026-123158 on systems? Successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to log in to a qualifying account without knowing its password. The resulting impact depends on that account’s permissions. Compromise of a service or standard account can expose data and application resources, while access to an account with doas, sudo, or equivalent privileges can potentially lead to complete system compromise. Can CVE-2026-123158 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Vulnerable OpenSSH installations remain exposed until patched or password authentication is disabled. The highest-risk systems are musl-based Linux environments such as Alpine Linux running sshd without PAM and containing qualifying passwordless accounts. Public reproduction material exists, although no confirmed exploitation in the wild has been reported as of November 6, 2026. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-123158? Upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distribution’s patched package and restart sshd. If patching cannot be completed immediately, disable password and keyboard-interactive authentication, restrict SSH exposure to trusted networks, and review successful password logins for suspicious activity. Administrators should continue monitoring vendor advisories for updated details for CVE-2026-123158 as exploitation intelligence evolves.

An attacker does not need to know the target user’s password. If an exposed SSH service meets the required conditions, an attacker who can reach the service can authenticate to certain accounts using a password in the vulnerable length range. The impact depends on the privileges assigned to the compromised account. Access to a privileged service account or an account capable of using doas or another privilege escalation mechanism could lead to full system compromise.

Contact Sales

OpenSSH addressed the issue in Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2, released on November 5, 2026. Alpine Linux simultaneously released patched OpenSSH packages for all supported branches and several older branches. The OpenSSH team describes the release as containing a critical security workaround for Linux systems using musl libc with PAM disabled.

Public reproduction environments and proof-of-concept material are already available. However, as of November 6, 2026, the reviewed sources do not report confirmed exploitation of the vulnerability in real-world attacks, and the flaw has not been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Organizations can strengthen defenses against emerging authentication bypass vulnerabilities with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, accelerating threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Security teams can also use Prime Architect to transform vulnerability intelligence into hunting queries and detection logic tailored to their available SSH, authentication, endpoint, and network telemetry.

Detect CVE-2026-123158 by monitoring successful password-based SSH logins to accounts that normally use key-only authentication, unusual authentication attempts containing abnormally long passwords, unexpected remote access to service accounts, and post-authentication activity inconsistent with the account’s normal behavior.

Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added.

CVE-2026-123158 analysis

CVE-2026-123158 affects OpenSSH sshd before Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 when it runs on Linux with musl libc and password authentication occurs without PAM. The CVE carries a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 with the vector AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H, reflecting remote exploitation without prior privileges or user interaction but requiring a specific system and account configuration.

The root cause lies in the interaction between OpenSSH and the password hashing function provided by musl libc.

On systems where PAM is disabled, sshd performs password validation using the system’s crypt() functionality. For a typical account, /etc/shadow contains a cryptographic password hash, and the value generated from the user’s submitted password is compared against that stored hash.

musl libc behaves differently when the supplied password exceeds its supported input length. For passwords longer than 256 bytes, crypt() returns * as an error value rather than a normal password hash.

The problem arises because * is also commonly used in /etc/shadow for accounts that do not have a traditional password configured.

If a vulnerable sshd receives an overlong password for one of these accounts, the authentication flow can effectively compare the * returned by crypt() with the * stored in the account’s shadow entry. The values match, and authentication can incorrectly succeed.

The CVE description states that, for affected account configurations, passwords between 256 and 1024 characters can result in successful authentication. Independent reproductions describe passwords exceeding the normal 256-byte boundary as sufficient to trigger the vulnerable condition.

The flaw is therefore not a universal password bypass affecting every OpenSSH deployment.

Several specific conditions must align.

First, the server must use musl libc. Alpine Linux is the primary mainstream example, although other embedded or minimal Linux environments can also use musl.

Second, sshd must authenticate users without PAM. Alpine’s standard openssh-server package is built without PAM, while the alternative openssh-server-pam configuration is protected when UsePAM yes is enabled.

Third, password authentication must be enabled. PasswordAuthentication yes is the relevant configuration. Systems configured for public-key-only authentication with PasswordAuthentication no are not exposed to the documented attack path.

Finally, the attacker needs an account whose password field contains *. These can include key-only users, accounts created without passwords, some identities provided through directory services, and certain cloud-image users.

Alpine also notes an additional condition: at least one local account must contain a $5$ or $6$-style password hash for the vulnerable authentication path to operate as described.

The root account deserves special attention. Alpine commonly stores root:*, but OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password prevents password authentication directly to root. As a result, a standard Alpine installation does not automatically expose direct root login through this bug.

That protection does not eliminate the broader risk. If another account with * in its password field is remotely accessible and has administrative rights through doas, sudo, container capabilities, or other privileged mechanisms, successful authentication can still provide a path to complete system compromise.

Alpine’s official tiny-cloud images are particularly relevant. Security research identified versions where the alpine account could meet the vulnerable conditions and was also able to use doas to gain elevated privileges. This illustrates why defenders should evaluate account privileges rather than assuming the vulnerability provides either harmless user access or automatic root access in every environment.

glibc-based Linux distributions such as Debian, Ubuntu, and RHEL are not affected by this specific vulnerability because the vulnerable behavior depends on musl libc’s password hashing implementation. Systems using PAM for SSH password validation are likewise outside the documented vulnerable configuration.

Containers require similar qualification. Alpine is widely used as a container base image, but ordinary containers that do not run sshd are not vulnerable through this attack path. The primary concern is containers, appliances, development environments, or legacy workloads that explicitly install and expose an SSH server.

The CVE-2026-123158 PoC landscape has developed quickly. Public reproduction labs are referenced directly by the vulnerability record, demonstrating that defenders should assume the authentication bypass can be reproduced without access to private exploit research. This materially raises remediation urgency even though confirmed malicious exploitation has not yet been reported.

The vulnerability was reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. OpenSSH publicly released version 10.6p2 with the security workaround on November 5, 2026. The reviewed primary sources do not specify the exact date on which the researcher initially discovered or privately reported the issue.

The OpenSSH fix adds validation designed to prevent error values and invalid short password hashes from being accepted during password authentication. OpenSSH notes that it considers the underlying root cause to exist outside sshd, but because the condition can be exploited through the SSH server, the project implemented a defensive workaround in OpenSSH itself.

Alpine Linux has backported the correction across multiple branches:

Alpine branchFixed OpenSSH packageedge10.6_p2-r03.2410.3_p1-r23.2310.2_p1-r13.2210.0_p1-r113.219.9_p2-r13.209.7_p1-r63.199.6_p1-r33.189.3_p2-r43.179.1_p1-r73.169.0_p1-r6

Administrators should rely on their distribution package status rather than the SSH version banner alone. Linux distributions frequently backport security patches without changing the upstream OpenSSH version displayed during the SSH handshake. A server displaying an older version string may therefore already contain the vendor fix.

For CVE-2026-123158 detection, defenders should prioritize SSH authentication telemetry. A particularly strong hunting signal is a successful password login to an account that is intended to use only public-key authentication or that has no usable password configured.

On Alpine systems, administrators can review /var/log/messages, centralized authentication logs, SIEM records, or equivalent telemetry for Accepted password events involving unexpected service, key-only, or administrative accounts.

Defenders should correlate successful authentication with source IP addresses, login times, session duration, commands executed after login, privilege elevation, changes to authorized_keys, account creation, scheduled jobs, and unexpected outbound network connections.

Network telemetry can also help identify exposed systems. Externally reachable SSH services advertising password or keyboard-interactive authentication should receive higher remediation priority, particularly when the underlying system is Alpine or another musl-based distribution.

At present, there are no campaign-specific CVE-2026-123158 IOCs such as confirmed attacker IP addresses, domains, malware hashes, or command-and-control infrastructure. The absence of static indicators makes behavioral monitoring of SSH authentication and subsequent session activity particularly important.

CVE-2026-123158 Mitigation

The primary remediation is to install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the corrected package supplied by the Linux distribution. Alpine administrators should update the full system using the current package repositories and restart sshd afterward. Updating the package alone does not replace the already running SSH daemon process.

Organizations running Alpine-based containers should rebuild and redeploy any image that installs openssh-server. Simply updating the host operating system does not patch vulnerable OpenSSH packages embedded inside container images.

Administrators should also identify exposure before assuming that every Alpine host is vulnerable. Key checks include:

  1. Determine whether the host uses musl libc.
  2. Verify whether sshd is running with PAM disabled.
  3. Check whether password authentication is enabled.
  4. Identify login-capable accounts whose /etc/shadow password field is *.
  5. Review the privileges assigned to those accounts.
  6. Confirm the installed OpenSSH package against the distribution’s corrected package version.

If immediate patching is impossible, organizations should disable SSH password authentication.

Configure:

PasswordAuthentication no

and, where applicable:

KbdInteractiveAuthentication no

Administrators should confirm that public-key authentication works before applying this configuration to avoid losing legitimate administrative access.

The SSH configuration should then be validated and the daemon reloaded or restarted. Afterward, external verification should confirm that the server offers only public-key authentication.

Restricting network accessibility provides additional defense in depth. SSH should generally be reachable only from trusted administrative networks, VPN infrastructure, bastion hosts, or explicit source-IP allowlists rather than being universally exposed to the internet.

Organizations should also reconsider whether SSH is required inside containers at all. Modern orchestration environments usually provide alternatives such as docker exec or kubectl exec, eliminating an unnecessary remotely reachable authentication service.

For potentially exposed systems, review historical successful password logins occurring before remediation. Pay particular attention to accounts configured without passwords and identities normally expected to authenticate exclusively with SSH keys.

If an unexpected successful login is identified, treat the account as potentially compromised. Review shell history where available, process execution, privilege escalation, new or modified authorized_keys entries, user and group changes, cron jobs, startup scripts, package installation, and outbound network connections.

Credentials and keys accessible to the compromised account should be considered potentially exposed and rotated according to the findings of the investigation. If the account had administrative privileges, defenders should expand the investigation to the entire host and any systems reachable using credentials stored there.

Public proof-of-concept material means organizations should not wait for evidence of widespread attacks before applying the fix. The exploitation prerequisites narrow the vulnerable population, but systems that meet those conditions can be accessed remotely without knowledge of a valid password.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-123158 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-123158 is a password authentication bypass affecting OpenSSH sshd on Linux systems using musl libc without PAM. When an excessively long password is passed to musl’s crypt() function, it can return * as an error value. If the target account also has * stored in /etc/shadow, vulnerable sshd configurations can incorrectly treat the values as matching and allow authentication.

When was CVE-2026-123158 first discovered?

The vulnerability was reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. OpenSSH published the security fix in Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 on November 5, 2026, and the CVE became public the same day. The currently reviewed primary advisories do not disclose the exact date of the researcher’s original private discovery.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-123158 on systems?

Successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to log in to a qualifying account without knowing its password. The resulting impact depends on that account’s permissions. Compromise of a service or standard account can expose data and application resources, while access to an account with doas, sudo, or equivalent privileges can potentially lead to complete system compromise.

Can CVE-2026-123158 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Vulnerable OpenSSH installations remain exposed until patched or password authentication is disabled. The highest-risk systems are musl-based Linux environments such as Alpine Linux running sshd without PAM and containing qualifying passwordless accounts. Public reproduction material exists, although no confirmed exploitation in the wild has been reported as of November 6, 2026.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-123158?

Upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distribution’s patched package and restart sshd. If patching cannot be completed immediately, disable password and keyboard-interactive authentication, restrict SSH exposure to trusted networks, and review successful password logins for suspicious activity. Administrators should continue monitoring vendor advisories for updated details for CVE-2026-123158 as exploitation intelligence evolves.



The post CVE-2026-123158: OpenSSH Password Authentication Bypass Affects Alpine Linux appeared first on SOC Prime.

items.title: Attacks on supermarket and blood storage systems prompt US warning
items.summary: Attackers don’t have to steal information to cause serious harm. Sometimes, changing a temperature setting is enough. On November 5, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and three other federal agencies issued a warning urging operators to secure industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems. The warning follows cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe. Separately, France’s national blood service confirmed that the monitoring and control systems at three of its cold-storage sites had been affected. Staff intervened before any blood products or samples were compromised. The incident showed how a connected cooling system can put essential supplies at risk. On October 13, after the first attacks in France , refrigeration supplier Danfoss advised its Dutch customers to disconnect their systems from the public internet and reconnect only through a secure network. A Danfoss spokesperson told NOS that most stores followed the advice. When similar attacks reached the Netherlands on November 2, major supermarket chains were reportedly unaffected. At least 17 businesses, mainly butcher shops and small neighborhood stores, had their refrigeration systems compromised. Danfoss said that the affected systems were still accessible through unsecured connections and used default passwords. The spokesperson said the attacks could have been prevented if the recommended precautions had been taken. CISA and its partners warned that attackers may exploit authentication bypass flaws, code-injection vulnerabilities, or weak configurations in refrigeration controllers. Successful attacks could let them change temperatures or force equipment into continuous heating or defrost cycles. The agencies recommend reducing that risk by keeping control panels off the public internet, isolating operational equipment from business networks, changing default passwords, using strong authentication, patching firmware , and replacing unsupported devices. They also recommend setting safe operating limits and alerts for temperature changes outside those limits. What about home appliances? You don’t need an industrial refrigeration unit to adopt some of these precautions. Check whether you need remote access. If you never use a device while away from home, disable that feature. Check the manufacturer’s instructions first; disabling remote access may also affect alerts or smart-home integrations. Check who can access the appliance, including suppliers, and how that access is protected. Change default passwords and secure the associated account. Use a strong password and enable two-step verification wherever the appliance or app supports it. Protecting the app account matters as well as protecting the appliance itself. Keep firmware and apps updated. Turn on automatic updates where available, and don’t ignore manual update prompts. “One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” According to CNET. Read their review →

Attackers don’t have to steal information to cause serious harm. Sometimes, changing a temperature setting is enough.

On November 5, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and three other federal agencies issued a warning urging operators to secure industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems.

The warning follows cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe. Separately, France’s national blood service confirmed that the monitoring and control systems at three of its cold-storage sites had been affected. Staff intervened before any blood products or samples were compromised. The incident showed how a connected cooling system can put essential supplies at risk.

On October 13, after the first attacks in France, refrigeration supplier Danfoss advised its Dutch customers to disconnect their systems from the public internet and reconnect only through a secure network.

A Danfoss spokesperson told NOS that most stores followed the advice. When similar attacks reached the Netherlands on November 2, major supermarket chains were reportedly unaffected. At least 17 businesses, mainly butcher shops and small neighborhood stores, had their refrigeration systems compromised.

Danfoss said that the affected systems were still accessible through unsecured connections and used default passwords. The spokesperson said the attacks could have been prevented if the recommended precautions had been taken.

CISA and its partners warned that attackers may exploit authentication bypass flaws, code-injection vulnerabilities, or weak configurations in refrigeration controllers. Successful attacks could let them change temperatures or force equipment into continuous heating or defrost cycles.

The agencies recommend reducing that risk by keeping control panels off the public internet, isolating operational equipment from business networks, changing default passwords, using strong authentication, patching firmware, and replacing unsupported devices. They also recommend setting safe operating limits and alerts for temperature changes outside those limits.

What about home appliances?

You don’t need an industrial refrigeration unit to adopt some of these precautions.

  • Check whether you need remote access. If you never use a device while away from home, disable that feature. Check the manufacturer’s instructions first; disabling remote access may also affect alerts or smart-home integrations.
  • Check who can access the appliance, including suppliers, and how that access is protected.
  • Change default passwords and secure the associated account. Use a strong password and enable two-step verification wherever the appliance or app supports it. Protecting the app account matters as well as protecting the appliance itself.
  • Keep firmware and apps updated. Turn on automatic updates where available, and don’t ignore manual update prompts.

items.title: After Binance, check what your signing systems can approve
items.summary: Binance’s October 2026 security incident raises an operational question for every organization holding user funds: Can your security controls recognize when a valid signature grants an attacker wallet authority? If an organization only monitors transfers and ownership changes, it may miss the shift in wallet authority until assets move. Binance’s initial update about the incident suggested that a compromised DevOps laptop allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawals. Its second update reported additional breaches but no evidence that wallet private keys had leaked. In its November 3 report , Binance described a broader attack involving social engineering, misuse of an internal AI tool, stolen credentials, and unauthorized access to its wallet-signing service. The attacker nevertheless obtained valid signatures, illustrating a major risk: a compromised server with permission to request signatures can misuse a protected key without extracting it. The attacker used an EIP-7702 delegation that allows a wallet to sign a standing instruction: “Use this code when my account is called.” Ethereum keeps that instruction in place until it is changed or cleared using the wallet’s key. That enabled repeated transfers , including funds deposited after the first theft, without further signatures from Binance. Other Binance wallets were drained through ordinary signed transfers. Transaction execution and monitoring systems must keep pace with Ethereum. EIP-7702 places delegation authorizations outside ordinary calldata. Session keys, recovery paths, authorization modules, Safe modules, and ERC-4337 UserOperations all add execution paths that signing policies and monitors must understand. Systems that have not been updated can miss malicious authority changes and asset movements, leaving wallets exposed. Teams must update their detection rules and test that these attack paths are covered. If you’re responsible for securing wallet infrastructure, start with our checklist. Four steps to strengthen wallet security These four recommendations address the risks exposed by the attack. We also provide tests to help you verify that these security controls work. 1. Reduce access to signing infrastructure Document every service and API that can request wallet signatures, who can call it, and what it can authorize, including transfers, delegation, and arbitrary data. Review this inventory whenever wallet functionality changes on supported chains. Separate signing infrastructure from everyday business systems and verify transaction details through an independent system. Use our TRAIL method to trace how a compromised laptop or server could reach signing. Verify the result: For each identified compromise path, use the access and credentials available to the compromised system to attempt an unapproved action. Identify the control expected to block it and retain evidence that no usable signature was produced. 2. Treat delegation as an administrative privilege Configure signing services to recognize requests that change account authority. Reject EIP-7702 authorizations for custody externally owned accounts (EOAs) that do not need delegation, and ensure generic digest-signing APIs cannot bypass that restriction. Where delegation is required, separately approve the authorizing account, delegate address and code, chain, and nonce. Before evaluating execution, simulations must apply the proposed delegation and inspect changes to permissions and future execution authority alongside immediate balance changes. Verify the result: Delegation requests for accounts with delegation disabled are rejected through both dedicated and generic signing interfaces. Changing an approved account, delegate, chain, or nonce requires renewed approval. Simulations expose added authority even when the transaction moves no assets immediately. 3. Limit damage even if signing is compromised Even after delegation, the original EOA key can still transfer funds or change the delegate. This means that if the key is compromised, an attacker can bypass limits enforced by the delegate. Protect those assets with separate custody controls that the operational key cannot change. Our cold-storage guidance describes independently enforced limits, monitored delays on sensitive actions, and a separate configuration authority. Verify the result: Treat the operational key as compromised and attempt direct transfers, delegate replacement, and policy changes. Confirm these paths cannot bypass the claimed protections, including shortening or removing delays. Exercise incident response against a malicious withdrawal. Record alert and containment times, and demonstrate that responders can cancel or contain the withdrawal before execution. Confirm that the blocked withdrawal cannot subsequently execute. 4. Detect changes in wallet authority Map each wallet to the assets and contracts it controls, including wallets that hold no funds. Alerts should identify the affected systems and privileges (e.g., an unapproved delegation on an account that can upgrade funded vaults). Attribute direct calls, module execution, and ERC-4337 operations to their authorization paths. Verify the result: Test various delegation scenarios, mixed authorization tuples, multisig-module execution, and failed UserOperations inside successful bundles. Monitoring should reconstruct authority changes and asset movements in order, identify affected systems, and distinguish detection from controls that block execution before funds move. Make signing infrastructure an ongoing responsibility If your organization runs wallets or signing services, take another look at how they’re secured. Test whether your signing policies account for EIP-7702 and ERC-4337, whether independent safeguards still work if an attacker gains access to signing, and whether your monitoring catches changes to accounts and permissions. Give someone ownership of this review and put it on a regular schedule. Run it again whenever you change the protocols you support, the wallets you use, or your signing services.

items.title: Faster LLM inference startup: What you need to know
items.summary: Adding an inference replica creates capacity only after the new instance can serve requests. Between starting a process and generating a response, an LLM server may need to load weights, initialize GPU resources, compile kernels, capture execution graphs, and warm up the engine. Restarts, model switches, and scale-out can repeat this work. The community is addressing these costs at several levels. vLLM and SGLang are developing ways to reuse weights and initialized state. Serving platforms are building workflows around warm instances and snapshots. Kubernetes, container runtimes, and the Open Container Initiative (OCI) are working on related interfaces and artifact questions. These efforts have different boundaries and are progressing independently. Understanding what each approach preserves helps explain both its benefits and its current scope. Why starting an inference server takes time A typical startup includes several kinds of work. The server launches processes and imports libraries. It reads model files, constructs tensors, and performs any required weight transformations. It initializes the execution runtime and communication between workers, allocates memory, and prepares the engine to serve. Some work happens specifically to improve subsequent inference performance. Compilation produces executable kernels; autotuning selects implementations for a configuration. CUDA Graph capture records GPU operations for later replay with lower launch overhead. The vLLM optimization documentation describes the tradeoff between startup work and steady-state execution performance. The balance depends on the model, software, hardware, and storage. Once model files are cached locally, engine initialization may become more visible. Once weights can be reused in GPU memory, imports, tuning, and graph capture may account for more of the remaining delay. What can be reused instead of rebuilt Startup optimizations can be grouped by the work they preserve: What is reused Approach Representative projects or features Work that can remain Model files Pre-staging and efficient loaders llm-d model caches, fastsafetensors Weight processing and initialization Compiled artifacts and tuning results Persistent caches vLLM compilation and autotune caches Runtime setup and graph capture Processed weights Daemons and weight transfer vLLM preload, SGLang weight cache, ModelExpress Construction of the rest of the engine A live engine Sleep/wake and warm instances vLLM sleep, SGLang memory saver, llm-d FMA Restoring released resources Initialized execution state Engine or container snapshots vLLM snapshots, SGLang snapshot proposal, Snapshot, llm-d/GKE Validation, restoration, and recovery work These approaches can appear together in a system, with integration conditions specific to each implementation. For example, an engine might reuse compiled artifacts while loading weights through a specialized loader. A snapshot workflow might discard an empty key/value (KV) cache before capture and recreate it after restoration. This cache holds attention state computed while processing tokens. Efficient loading remains a separate area of work. SGLang documents loaders such as pre-sharded state, fastsafetensors, and streaming loaders. llm-d documents model-file caches alongside other startup paths. These mechanisms affect how weights reach an engine; they preserve different states from a snapshot of an initialized process. SGLang model loading , llm-d startup overview . What vLLM and SGLang are doing vLLM vLLM’s Fast Start work centers on a persistent weight daemon. It loads and processes weights, holds the resulting tensors in GPU memory, and exposes them to compatible engines through CUDA inter-process communication. The weight-daemon implementation and the vllm preload command have been merged. Current preload documentation also describes preparing FlashInfer autotune results before an engine starts. Fast Start implementation , preload documentation . This separates the lifetime of cached weights from an engine restart. In the zero-copy mode, an engine maps the daemon’s existing allocations. Configuration checks determine whether reuse is appropriate, and the documented path can fall back to ordinary loading. The daemon must remain alive while engines use its memory. CUDA IPC handles are local to a node; documented multi-node deployments provide the relevant shards locally on each node. vLLM also has sleep/wake support, which retains a live server while releasing much of its GPU memory. That provides a different lifecycle from starting a new engine against cached weights. The preload documentation identifies restrictions on combining its zero-copy mode with weight offloading through sleep mode. Sleep mode . A separate, merged implementation adds experimental initialized-engine snapshots. The vllm snapshot workflow uses CRIU to capture and restore Linux process state, with CUDA checkpoint support handling GPU state. Its documented scope requires the same machine and compatible environment, with one NVIDIA GPU and tensor parallelism of one. It releases weights and KV state before capture and reloads them during restoration, retaining a dependency on the model files. Restoration also checks a recorded generation result. Initialized engine snapshots . SGLang SGLang has merged a weight-cache daemon that holds processed weights and shares them with new engine instances through CUDA IPC. Its Fast Engine Recovery roadmap discusses extending this foundation, including broader model and quantization coverage, memory transport, daemon lifecycle, and remaining initialization costs. The roadmap describes directions beyond the merged initial implementation. Weight-cache implementation , Fast Engine Recovery roadmap . SGLang also exposes memory release/resume and generation pause/continue operations used by external snapshot integrations. Whether weights remain available after release depends on the configured memory policy, including CPU backup. These operations let integrations prepare an engine for capture and resume it afterward; the surrounding workflow still needs to coordinate them. Initialized-engine snapshots are another direction. The open RFC and implementation PR propose capturing SGLang after initialization and before its HTTP service binds. Their initial scope is one NVIDIA GPU, tensor parallelism of one, and the same host and software environment. Model weights remain external and are reloaded after restore. Initialization snapshot RFC , implementation PR . Both frameworks also have open proposals about cooperating with an external checkpoint orchestrator. The engine would prepare its own state and resume serving; the external system would capture, store, and restore the process. These proposals address a practical boundary: a node agent can operate checkpoint tools, while the inference engine knows when its requests, caches, and communication resources are safe to capture. vLLM proposal , SGLang proposal . How platforms turn mechanisms into startup workflows Snapshot and Dynamo The independent Snapshot project in the ai-dynamo organization provides checkpoint and restore primitives for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. items.summary_html:
Adding an inference replica creates capacity only after the new instance can serve requests. Between starting a process and generating a response, an LLM server may need to load weights, initialize GPU resources, compile kernels, capture execution graphs, and warm up the engine. Restarts, model switches, and scale-out can repeat this work.

The community is addressing these costs at several levels. vLLM and SGLang are developing ways to reuse weights and initialized state. Serving platforms are building workflows around warm instances and snapshots. Kubernetes, container runtimes, and the Open Container Initiative (OCI) are working on related interfaces and artifact questions.

These efforts have different boundaries and are progressing independently. Understanding what each approach preserves helps explain both its benefits and its current scope.

Why starting an inference server takes time

A typical startup includes several kinds of work. The server launches processes and imports libraries. It reads model files, constructs tensors, and performs any required weight transformations. It initializes the execution runtime and communication between workers, allocates memory, and prepares the engine to serve.

Some work happens specifically to improve subsequent inference performance. Compilation produces executable kernels; autotuning selects implementations for a configuration. CUDA Graph capture records GPU operations for later replay with lower launch overhead. The vLLM optimization documentation describes the tradeoff between startup work and steady-state execution performance.

The balance depends on the model, software, hardware, and storage. Once model files are cached locally, engine initialization may become more visible. Once weights can be reused in GPU memory, imports, tuning, and graph capture may account for more of the remaining delay.

What can be reused instead of rebuilt

Startup optimizations can be grouped by the work they preserve:

What is reusedApproachRepresentative projects or featuresWork that can remainModel filesPre-staging and efficient loadersllm-d model caches, fastsafetensorsWeight processing and initializationCompiled artifacts and tuning resultsPersistent cachesvLLM compilation and autotune cachesRuntime setup and graph captureProcessed weightsDaemons and weight transfervLLM preload, SGLang weight cache, ModelExpressConstruction of the rest of the engineA live engineSleep/wake and warm instancesvLLM sleep, SGLang memory saver, llm-d FMARestoring released resourcesInitialized execution stateEngine or container snapshotsvLLM snapshots, SGLang snapshot proposal, Snapshot, llm-d/GKEValidation, restoration, and recovery work

These approaches can appear together in a system, with integration conditions specific to each implementation. For example, an engine might reuse compiled artifacts while loading weights through a specialized loader. A snapshot workflow might discard an empty key/value (KV) cache before capture and recreate it after restoration. This cache holds attention state computed while processing tokens.

Efficient loading remains a separate area of work. SGLang documents loaders such as pre-sharded state, fastsafetensors, and streaming loaders. llm-d documents model-file caches alongside other startup paths. These mechanisms affect how weights reach an engine; they preserve different states from a snapshot of an initialized process. SGLang model loading, llm-d startup overview.

What vLLM and SGLang are doing vLLM

vLLM’s Fast Start work centers on a persistent weight daemon. It loads and processes weights, holds the resulting tensors in GPU memory, and exposes them to compatible engines through CUDA inter-process communication. The weight-daemon implementation and the vllm preload command have been merged. Current preload documentation also describes preparing FlashInfer autotune results before an engine starts. Fast Start implementation, preload documentation.

This separates the lifetime of cached weights from an engine restart. In the zero-copy mode, an engine maps the daemon’s existing allocations. Configuration checks determine whether reuse is appropriate, and the documented path can fall back to ordinary loading. The daemon must remain alive while engines use its memory. CUDA IPC handles are local to a node; documented multi-node deployments provide the relevant shards locally on each node.

vLLM also has sleep/wake support, which retains a live server while releasing much of its GPU memory. That provides a different lifecycle from starting a new engine against cached weights. The preload documentation identifies restrictions on combining its zero-copy mode with weight offloading through sleep mode. Sleep mode.

A separate, merged implementation adds experimental initialized-engine snapshots. The vllm snapshot workflow uses CRIU to capture and restore Linux process state, with CUDA checkpoint support handling GPU state. Its documented scope requires the same machine and compatible environment, with one NVIDIA GPU and tensor parallelism of one. It releases weights and KV state before capture and reloads them during restoration, retaining a dependency on the model files. Restoration also checks a recorded generation result. Initialized engine snapshots.

SGLang

SGLang has merged a weight-cache daemon that holds processed weights and shares them with new engine instances through CUDA IPC. Its Fast Engine Recovery roadmap discusses extending this foundation, including broader model and quantization coverage, memory transport, daemon lifecycle, and remaining initialization costs. The roadmap describes directions beyond the merged initial implementation. Weight-cache implementation, Fast Engine Recovery roadmap.

SGLang also exposes memory release/resume and generation pause/continue operations used by external snapshot integrations. Whether weights remain available after release depends on the configured memory policy, including CPU backup. These operations let integrations prepare an engine for capture and resume it afterward; the surrounding workflow still needs to coordinate them.

Initialized-engine snapshots are another direction. The open RFC and implementation PR propose capturing SGLang after initialization and before its HTTP service binds. Their initial scope is one NVIDIA GPU, tensor parallelism of one, and the same host and software environment. Model weights remain external and are reloaded after restore. Initialization snapshot RFC, implementation PR.

Both frameworks also have open proposals about cooperating with an external checkpoint orchestrator. The engine would prepare its own state and resume serving; the external system would capture, store, and restore the process. These proposals address a practical boundary: a node agent can operate checkpoint tools, while the inference engine knows when its requests, caches, and communication resources are safe to capture. vLLM proposal, SGLang proposal.

How platforms turn mechanisms into startup workflows Snapshot and Dynamo

The independent Snapshot project in the ai-dynamo organization provides checkpoint and restore primitives for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. Its operator and node agent coordinate CRIU and CUDA checkpoint operations, with resources such as PodSnapshot and SnapshotJob. Dynamo integrates these primitives into its serving workflows. Snapshot project.

Snapshot’s documented storage path uses a shared persistent volume accessible by node agents. Agent-side components manage artifact movement and restore access. Its current storage documentation supports storage through a Kubernetes PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC); object-storage backends are reserved for future use. Hardware, driver, runtime, and workload compatibility still constrain restoration. Storage model.

The framework examples also show the application work involved. The SGLang example mounts an entrypoint that warms the engine, pauses generation, releases memory, and signals that capture is safe. After restoration, it resumes memory and generation, validates a generation, and starts its API. The vLLM guide validates its own entrypoint on v0.27.1 and explicitly says that example does not work on v0.28. This illustrates a compatibility boundary for that integration. SGLang guide, vLLM guide.

Dynamo separately develops GPU Memory Service, which moves GPU-memory ownership outside the engine process. Its integration and snapshot support need to be read by version: Dynamo’s v1.4.0 Snapshot documentation explicitly describes GMS plus Snapshot as disabled and unsupported for production. GPU Memory Service, versioned Snapshot documentation.

llm-d

llm-d documents several startup approaches. Its Pod Snapshots guide currently covers single-GPU vLLM and SGLang deployments using GKE Pod Snapshots, GKE Sandbox based on gVisor, and Google Cloud Storage. The initial instance loads and warms the model, prepares its memory, and triggers a snapshot. Compatible later Pods restore that state and resume the framework. The guide describes a platform-independent CRIU backend as work in progress. Pod Snapshots guide.

This backend differs from Snapshot’s CRIU path. gVisor saves sandbox state through its own checkpoint mechanism; GKE documents GPU-state capture through NVIDIA checkpoint support. Similar high-level workflows therefore do not imply identical checkpoint formats or APIs. GKE Pod snapshots.

Fast Model Actuation takes another approach. It uses controllers and a requester/launcher Pod arrangement to manage vLLM instances. Depending on available state and placement, it can wake a sleeping instance or start one through a launcher that has already loaded Python modules. Its hot path depends on matching the retained instance to the assigned GPU. FMA guide.

llm-d also documents ModelExpress for transferring weights from a seed replica to peers using NIXL and remote direct memory access (RDMA) over a compatible network. This changes weight distribution while leaving other engine-startup work to the receiving instance. These three paths illustrate why a platform’s startup work cannot be represented by a single checkpoint feature. ModelExpress integration.

Where Kubernetes checkpoint and restore stands

The Kubernetes Checkpoint Restore Working Group provides a place to coordinate use cases, API proposals, and integration with SIGs and runtimes. Its charter also identifies checkpoint archive efficiency as an area to revisit. The group’s scope concerns platform orchestration; inference frameworks continue to develop their internal startup mechanisms independently. Working-group charter.

Kubernetes already has container checkpointing through the work associated with Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal (KEP) 2008, which reached beta in v1.30. KEP-5823 addresses Pod-level checkpoint and restore. It is marked implementable with a v1.38 alpha target; that milestone is a delivery target. Its initial boundaries exclude device state and cross-node restore. GPU support has a separate provisional proposal, KEP-6274, whose enhancement PR remains open and discusses device allocation and compatibility. Container checkpoint API, Pod-level proposal, GPU proposal.

There is concrete progress at the Container Runtime Interface, or CRI, boundary. The PR adding CheckpointPod and RestorePod merged on July 22, 2026. The current interface describes consistent capture, resumption after checkpointing, and cleanup on restore failure. Restore prepares containers before their execution starts. The Kubernetes orchestration and containerd implementation PRs remain open; CRI-O’s implementation PR is a draft. CRI API change, Kubernetes implementation, containerd implementation, CRI-O implementation.

CRI leaves checkpoint files and their layout to the runtime. OCI addresses a different concern: packaging and distribution. Its image specification supports generic artifacts, and its distribution specification provides registry transfer and referrers mechanisms. These facilities can carry checkpoint payloads without defining their execution-state semantics. OCI artifact guidance, OCI distribution specification.

The checkpoint-specific OCI image proposal, issue #962, remains open. Podman can create checkpoint images, checkpointctl can build OCI-compatible images from checkpoint archives, and containerd has its own checkpoint media types. These are existing packaging practices alongside an unresolved proposal for a common definition. Registry storage alone does not establish restore compatibility across runtimes or GPU environments. Checkpoint image proposal, checkpointctl, containerd media types.

Directions being explored

The roadmaps cover several remaining costs. vLLM’s Fast Start work includes weight-cache validation, tuning, process startup, profiling, and graph-capture questions. SGLang’s Fast Engine Recovery roadmap includes broader model coverage, memory transport, daemon lifecycle, and initialization beyond weight loading. Their task lists describe directions; individual implementations carry their own status and supported configurations.

Snapshot lifecycle proposals also explore how applications report that capture is safe and how they learn that restoration has completed. The Snapshot project’s application-hooks design discusses files, HTTP, and Unix signals for these transitions. The framework proposals approach the same boundary from the engine side. Their existence does not establish a shared protocol already adopted across projects. Application lifecycle hooks proposal.

At the platform and runtime layers, ongoing work concerns Pod and GPU contracts, checkpoint artifacts, and compatibility. For readers following this area, the useful questions remain concrete: which work is preserved, which component owns it, what restoration still requires, and which environments the implementation supports.

  • SGLang Fast Engine Recovery roadmap: weight-cache evolution and other startup costs under discussion.

items.title: Storm-2603 Hackers Exploit SharePoint ToolShell Flaws to Hide Fileless Backdoor and Launch Ransomware Attack
items.summary: A China-linked threat group tracked as Storm-2603 has used the SharePoint ToolShell flaws to plant a backdoor that never touches the disk. The group then tried to run Warlock ransomware on the same network. The break-in hit an on-premises SharePoint server and ended with a ransomware launch that security software blocked. ToolShell is the name for a set of Microsoft SharePoint bugs, including CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771. They let an attacker run code on a server through specially crafted web requests. Microsoft linked the ransomware side of this activity to Storm-2603, while other groups using the same flaws mostly stole data and spied. Defenders who thought July 2025 patching closed the story should note that unpatched servers were still being hit months later. Researchers at Securelist , the threat research arm of Kaspersky, identified and documented this intrusion in a report published on November 5, 2026. Their team found the activity in a December review of a customer’s logs. They noted that the attackers kept control inside the IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, and wrote nothing to disk for the backdoor itself. You can read the full Securelist analysis for the technical details. Storm-2603 Hackers Exploit SharePoint ToolShell Flaws The first sign was small. On December 20, a single request hit a SharePoint ToolPane endpoint to check whether the host was vulnerable to CVE-2025-53770. It came from infrastructure tied to ONYPHE, an internet scanning platform. About 12 minutes later, a second connection arrived from a bulletproof hosting provider, Pfcloud UG. Nothing was exploited yet, and three quiet days followed. Because of that gap, the team first rated the probe as low priority. The real intrusion came on December 24, Christmas Eve, when many security teams run with fewer staff. Attack chain (Source – Securelist) The attacker sent a crafted request from 45.91.94[.]204, a Safing Privacy Network node that hides the true source behind several relays. That request loaded a webshell straight into the IIS worker process. It ran in memory and vanished if the application pool was recycled or IIS restarted. This matches what earlier reports on the ToolShell zero-day and Warlock ransomware warned about. The webshell was a modular C# framework. Its main part, G.cs, registered a custom VirtualPathProvider, which lets ASP.NET serve pages that do not exist as files. It woke up only when a request carried a specific User-Agent, so normal traffic never triggered it. It talked to the attacker over a custom binary protocol with simple XOR scrambling. It also used the suo5 proxy tool to tunnel traffic through the SharePoint host, which let the attackers reach other machines inside the network. Other modules listed running processes, logged-on users and network connections. One installed MSI packages silently, and another created admin accounts through low-level Windows account calls instead of normal commands. For SYSTEM rights, the code used a named-pipe trick copied from the EfsPotato tool, which works because IIS worker processes hold the needed impersonation privilege. Velociraptor, Tunnels and a Blocked Warlock Launch Soon after the webshell ran, the worker process started msiexec.exe to install a package from Supabase cloud storage. The package was Velociraptor version 0.73.4.0, a real forensics tool with a known flaw, CVE-2025-6264. Cisco Talos had already described Velociraptor abused in ransomware cases tied to the same group. Here, the attackers used it for persistence, discovery, data collection and running payloads. Through Velociraptor, they set up several backup routes: Zoho Assist, VS Code tunneling, Cloudflare Tunnel and a small reverse proxy. With so many paths, deleting one tool would not end their access. They also stopped depending on the webshell or the ToolShell bug at this point. The group then dropped a vulnerable driver, rsndispot.sys, to shut down endpoint protection. Fingerprinting with ONYPHE (Source – Securelist) A sideloaded DLL, flagged as Warlock’s antivirus killer, was likely meant to use it. This fits earlier findings on custom malware that abuses BYOVD from the same actor. The final step failed. Kaspersky’s Proactive Defense Module blocked the Warlock ransomware process before it could encrypt anything. Securelist assigns the case to Storm-2603 with moderate confidence, based on the ToolShell use, the Warlock tools and the Velociraptor habits. For defenders, patching is not enough. Install Microsoft’s emergency SharePoint security updates , then rotate exposed MachineKeys and hunt for persistence. Watch for odd w3wp.exe behavior, new VirtualPathProvider registrations, unexpected outbound connections and new remote-management tools. Securelist also advises keeping memory and IIS logs, and treating a confirmed exploit as a full host compromise.
