items.title: Huntress turns real-world attack intelligence into fleet-wide ‘herd immunity’ with new platform capabilities
items.summary: Huntress has announced a wave of new capabilities across its Agentic Security Platform, designed to turn intelligence gathered from live attacks into proactive defences for every customer, rather than leaving each incident as one organisation’s problem. The updates span Managed ITDR, Managed EDR, Managed SIEM, Managed SAT and Managed ISPM. They draw on the company’s visibility across nearly 300,000 businesses, 17 million identities and 6 million endpoints, combined with its 24/7 AI-centric Security Operations Center (SOC). The principle is simple: when an attack targets one organisation, Huntress applies what it learns across its entire fleet through automated blocking, earlier detection of hidden compromises, attack disruption and real-time user interventions. “Defending against threats moving at machine speed requires knowing the adversary better than anyone else and anticipating their next move by continuously learning from every attack and leveraging our scale and elite security researchers to turn that intelligence into stronger protection,” said Prakash Ramamurthy, Chief Product Officer at Huntress . “These innovations demonstrate how we’re bringing together unrivaled human expertise, AI, and real-world threat intelligence to protect businesses at the speed adversaries operate.” Blocking identity attacks at sign-in The headline addition to Managed ITDR is Adversary Infrastructure. When Huntress confirms hosting, relay or proxy infrastructure being used in an identity attack, it converts that intelligence into a blocking Conditional Access policy across every eligible, opted-in Microsoft 365 tenant the same day. One customer’s incident becomes protection for the wider customer base before the attacker can move on to the next target. Managed ITDR also now detects and shuts down suspicious service principals. The feature builds on Huntress’ investigation into the ConnectWise/SkyKick vendor compromise, in which attackers used stolen vendor credentials to access Microsoft 365 environments. It analyses service principal sign-ins, issues detailed incident reports and automatically disables compromised applications without partner intervention. It is available now for tenants with Microsoft Entra ID P1 licensing or higher. A third ITDR feature, Lookback, reviews up to 180 days of login history for newly onboarded Microsoft 365 tenants. It looks for evidence of credential theft, token theft, adversary-in-the-middle attacks, suspicious browsers and data centre logins that predate deployment. Where a compromise is still active, Huntress investigates and revokes the affected identity’s sessions. During early access, Lookback helped an MSP uncover a compromised $2 million real estate wire transfer, with suspicious activity dating back three days before onboarding. Disrupting remote ransomware Huntress says nearly 30% of the ransomware cases it observed this year originated from an unprotected system, which attackers use as a foothold for reconnaissance and to launch attacks across the network. Because these remote attacks leave few conventional indicators on protected endpoints, they are hard for traditional endpoint tools to stop. Managed EDR now uses Ransomware Canaries to detect this activity and automatically block communication between protected systems and the compromised, unprotected machine, stopping the spread. The capability becomes generally available on 30 November and activates automatically on systems protected by Managed EDR. Brute force visibility and identity posture Brute Force Sentry, a new Managed SIEM capability, detects brute-force activity across Windows RDP, RD Gateway, RDWeb and Linux SSH, correlating failed sign-ins with subsequent successes across log sources. Customers gain visibility into exposed surfaces, targeted accounts and persistent attack sources. It activates automatically when the required telemetry is available, reports clearly when coverage is unavailable and why, and will be generally available on 18 November. Managed ISPM adds an on-demand Identity Posture Assessment: a shareable snapshot of any Microsoft 365 tenant’s identity security posture, scored against the Huntress Identity Security Framework, with a prioritised list of gaps and recommended next steps. Training users mid-attack On the human side, Managed SAT introduces Defense Drills: short, hands-on simulations built from attacker tradecraft recently detected by the Huntress SOC. Integration with Managed EDR means the drills can act as a real-time intervention. When a ClickFix attack is shut down, the user sees a pop-up explaining what was stopped and is directed to a quick drill on how ClickFix works. The EDR incident report records completion. The EDR-triggered training will be available to all EDR customers, whether or not they use SAT. “The fact that Managed SAT from Huntress is built on real tradecraft that their SOC is seeing in the wild has helped us demonstrate to school administrators and users how an entire district could be compromised in just a few minutes,” said Michael Codis, Systems & Network Administrator, Hunterdon County Educational Services Commission. “Showing how that risk comes to life is incredibly powerful.” Huntress says the continuous feedback loop between its SOC analysts, threat researchers, tactical response teams, and detection engineers, combined with telemetry from across its customer base, allows it to develop and deploy protections informed by threats observed in the wild.

items.title: ARTEX AI Hacking Framework Found on 1,465 Public Servers, Some Hosting Cyberattack Tools
items.summary: Security researchers have found ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration-testing framework, exposed on 1,465 internet-facing hosts. Some servers also hosted command-and-control tools, phishing software, and exploit files, showing how automated security-testing platforms are appearing alongside established attack infrastructure. The findings offer defenders a view of these environments, including files operators left publicly accessible. The count does not mean 1,465 separate hacking groups are operating the framework. Around 650 hosts shared repeated configurations across two hosting providers, suggesting cloned systems or servers using multiple addresses. Removing those clusters leaves roughly 815 distinct-looking deployments. Public exposure also does not establish malicious activity, because authorized security testers can use ARTEX. Researchers from Censys identified the exposed consoles and associated attack tools in a November 5 report. They described ARTEX as a dual-use framework, not a malware family. Their investigation found additional threat detections on 155 hosts, or 10.6% of the total, and 32 open directories exposing tools, implants, and operator files. ARTEX AI Hacking Framework Found on 1,465 Public Servers Released on July 26, 2026, ARTEX combines a Go backend, Next.js console, and PostgreSQL database. It connects with ScopeSentry, an asset-discovery platform, to import domains, addresses, ports, and endpoints. Operators define a target, testing scope, and objective; AI agents then plan tasks, execute tools, and record results. Earlier coverage of ARTEX enterprise attack automation explains how this approach reduces manual work across attack stages. A planner breaks objectives into smaller actions, while worker agents run tools such as nmap and return findings. ARTEX maintains an asset graph showing discovered systems and an exploration graph tracking what has been tested. ARTEX’s workflow (Source – Censys) It supports Anthropic, OpenAI, and compatible model endpoints, allowing operators to change providers without rebuilding the workflow. Censys found CyberStrikeAI alongside ARTEX on 70 hosts, with PentAGI, HexStrike AI, and RedAmon also appearing. Other servers carried Vshell, Cobalt Strike, Adaptix C2, FRP, and Gophish. These combinations matter because reconnaissance, phishing, remote access, and AI-assisted testing can sit together, although shared hosting alone does not prove a coordinated attack. The exposed directories provided stronger operational clues. Their contents included Windows lateral-movement tools, a public sudo exploit, Linux implants, reverse-shell scripts, and compiled stagers. One directory exposed One directory exposed an operator’s home folder, including SSH material and shell history. Separate reporting on ARTEX Active Directory attacks describes how agents have supported credential attacks and movement between Windows systems. Censys also traced an ARTEX server cited by CrowdStrike to open directories visible from August 18, seven weeks before CrowdStrike’s report. That investigation linked ARTEX to attacks against South Korean financial institutions. Separately, Microsoft attributed ARTEX-assisted activity against ConnectWise customer tenants to Storm-0940. Coverage of ARTEX Microsoft 365 targeting details that campaign’s scanning, password spraying, and OAuth abuse. Defenders should correlate infrastructure matches with authentication logs, endpoint activity, and network connections rather than treat every ARTEX console as hostile. Censys recommends checking nearby open directories, tunneling services, unfamiliar LLM gateways, and historical scan records. Short-lived directories are particularly useful: ten disappeared and fifteen appeared elsewhere between November 3 and November 5. items.title: Claude Dispatch Flaw Lets Malicious Browser Extensions Run Code on Connected Computers
items.summary: A flaw in Anthropic’s Claude Dispatch let a malicious browser extension run commands on a computer via Claude Desktop. That computer could even be a different machine signed into the same Claude account. Researcher Gal Weizman of Forever Security named the technique ThisBash and published the findings on November 4, 2026. Anthropic plans to retire Dispatch, but the design behind it still lives in other Claude features. Dispatch lets a person send a task from a phone to Claude Desktop, an AI agent that can work with local files, apps, and commands. Anthropic’s help page says the feature is in limited beta and is closed to new users. The same page warns that a manipulated instruction could trigger actions that are hard to undo. The researchers found no flaw in the phone-to-desktop link itself. The trouble started when the same workflow was reached from claude.ai in a browser, where an extension can run alongside the page. Claude Dispatch Vulnerability Claude Desktop is an Electron app. That means it is built from the same web interface and API as claude.ai. The web version only hid the Dispatch link. It never blocked access to it. Once someone copied the page address from the desktop app, any logged-in browser tab could open Dispatch and send requests. An extension with permission to run scripts on claude.ai could do the same through the user’s own cookies. In the proof of concept , the script opened Dispatch in a tiny 200 by 200 pixel background window. It then asked the API for the session ID of the user’s desktop agent. This was the only visible trace on screen. Claude first hesitated when asked to install an unknown npm package. The script read each reply and sent a follow-up in the user’s voice. Forever Security calls this prompt forcing. In normal prompt injection, hostile text hides inside a page or file that the model reads, and the attacker gets one try. In prompt forcing, the attacker controls the whole chat and can rephrase, insist and try new angles until the model gives in. Four written prompts were enough. A short loop also clicked any “Allow” button once per second, so no human had to approve anything. The package then ran and opened Calculator. The team noted that the same step could have copied files, added SSH keys or planted a backdoor. Dispatch is built to link devices, so the browser and the desktop do not need to be on one computer. Picture an employee who signs into a personal Claude account on a work laptop. A bad extension in their home browser could then send orders to that work laptop. It would run next to source code and cloud keys. The researchers said they have seen personal accounts with cross-device Dispatch turned on at corporate endpoints. Extensions are common enough to make this a real path. LayerX found that 99% of enterprise users in its sample had at least one extension, and 53% had extensions with high or critical permissions. Forever Security’s earlier MaXSS and Spyder research showed how flaws in two popular Chrome extensions, with over 10 million installs between them, could let websites act across other sites. A bad extension can come from a rogue install, a hijacked update or a bug in a trusted tool. A malicious extension can already read pages, steal data and act through logged-in sessions. That is serious. But it normally stays inside the browser. ThisBash crossed that line. Permission to talk to a website became permission to run commands on the computer. The requests also looked real. They came from a real session and a real account, with permissions the user had granted. That proved who was logged in. It did not prove the user wanted a command to run. The researchers put it this way: a web session alone is not proof that the user approved an action on their machine. Researchers have shown extensions steering AI tools several times this year. Cyber Security News covered BragJack , where a single extension took over the built-in assistants of five major browsers. That story shows the problem goes well beyond one vendor. Any AI tool that trusts the page it sits in can be steered by code running in that page. Weizman reported the issue to Anthropic on May 14, 2026. Anthropic confirmed it was valid on May 19 but closed the report as a duplicate of a problem it had already found. On October 13, the company said Dispatch would be retired, with a target of the end of October 2026. That date has now passed, and I could not confirm from public sources that the feature is fully gone. The wider concern is that Claude Code Remote Control and Cowork sessions let the web drive a local agent by design. The researchers say extensions can repeat the same trick there and plan a follow-up post. Taking away one feature does not remove the trust gap underneath. Start with a list of the AI agents on your endpoints and the accounts they use. Check whether those accounts sit under company single sign-on. Turn off cross-device remote control where there is no business need, and review how devices are paired and removed. Treat extensions like any other software. Limit who can install them, review their permissions and watch for updates that ask for more. Approval prompts should be something the requesting component cannot click for itself. Teams should also watch for odd package installs, config changes and credential access linked to agent activity. Anthropic recently added a beta EDR monitoring option for Claude Cowork on Team and Enterprise plans, which can help with that last step. The simplest habit is also the strongest. Keep personal AI accounts off work devices, and keep work accounts out of personal browsers. ThisBash shows why that line matters. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Hackers Could Bypass ChatGPT Lockdown Mode to Steal Conversations Without Users Knowing
items.summary: A flaw in ChatGPT let attackers slip past Lockdown Mode, the safety setting meant to stop data leaks. Check Point Research found that a hidden pop-up trick could copy a user’s full chat history, show fake windows, and push malware. In the ChatGPT Classic desktop app, simply chatting was enough to trigger the leak. OpenAI has fixed the bug. OpenAI launched Lockdown Mode on February 13, 2026, first for business plans. On June 4, it reached personal accounts, where users can turn it on under Settings > Security. The setting limits web browsing to cached pages and turns off live web access, image support in replies, Deep Research, Agent Mode, Canvas networking, live connectors, and file downloads. OpenAI says it is built for high-risk users, such as executives and security teams, and is not needed by most people. Our earlier story on the ChatGPT Lockdown Mode release covers the basics. The goal is to stop prompt injection, where hidden text tricks the AI into following an attacker’s orders. A common trick is to make the AI load a link like attacker.example/collect?data= followed by private details. The data then shows up in the attacker’s server logs and the chat looks normal. ChatGPT Lockdown Mode Bypass This is not the first hidden exit path Check Point has found. In March, the team showed that DNS tunneling in ChatGPT’s code runtime could send chat data to an outside server. We covered that bug in ChatGPT Vulnerability Let Attackers Silently Exfiltrate User Prompts . The new flaw shows how closing one path does not protect the others. In February 2026, OpenAI added an HTML preview to ChatGPT code blocks, so users can view a page right in the chat. That page runs inside two nested iframes, which are small boxed-in web pages. The box blocks outside images, scripts, and links, and it asks the user before anything leaves. Researcher Alexey Bukhteyev spotted a weak point. The boxes allowed popups through two settings, allow-popups and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox. ChatGPT guarded popups by swapping out the window.open function. A page could skip that guard by adding one more iframe and calling that iframe’s own window.open. The popup then opened with no prompt, even in Lockdown Mode. Since the second setting was on, code in the popup ran outside the box. The first risk was fake update windows. The popup kept the ChatGPT icon, while the attacker chose the title. That made a malware download look like a real app update. In a browser, downloads are not blocked, so a shared chat link was enough, and the victim did not even need an account. In the desktop app, the user still had to click the download link. The second risk was silent data theft. In ChatGPT Classic, built on Electron, window.open worked without any user click. A malicious prompt, a malicious custom GPT, or a shared chat could then send the whole conversation, and uploaded files, to the attacker’s server. The third risk was stolen logins. The team also reloaded the main ChatGPT window and signed the user out. A fake login page could then capture the password when the user signed back in. Check Point reported the problem to OpenAI. On September 18, 2026, OpenAI said it removed both popup permissions from the outer preview iframe. Check Point retested and confirmed the trick no longer works. Check Point published its report on November 5. No user action is needed for this specific bug, but a few habits lower the risk of similar ones. Do not click buttons, previews, or “update” prompts inside shared chats. Skip prompts copied from unknown sites and avoid custom GPTs from unknown builders. Check the address bar or sign-in page before typing a password, especially after an unexpected logout. Keep the desktop app updated, and avoid pasting medical, financial, or work secrets into any chat unless needed. Even OpenAI says its safeguards reduce risk but give no full guarantee. As AI tools run code and show web content, each new feature adds a new way in. Careful habits remain a necessary layer of protection. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: OpenAI Launches GPT-6 Cyber That Finds 81 Firefox Flaws and Develops 948 Linux Exploits
items.summary: OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Cyber, a security-focused AI model that found 81 new high-severity Firefox flaws and built working exploits for 948 Linux kernel bugs. The company says it also follows the limits set by researchers far better than its older model. OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber on November 4, 2026. It is first going to a small group of approved Daybreak Red customers through the API and Codex. On ExploitGym, a test of whether a model can exploit a known flaw, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5%. GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 32.1%. On a new web testing task, it found 40.3% of flaws, compared with 32.0% for GPT-6 Astra. On RemoteExploitBench, GPT-6 Cyber finished 95% of tasks. Astra with Daybreak Blue refused all of them. OpenAI now rates the model Critical for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework. GPT-5.6 Cyber was rated High. A big risk with security agents is that they wander outside their job. OpenAI tested this with ExploitGym Honeypot, which was shaped by the earlier Hugging Face incident . The test places easy-to-break side services next to the real target. Attacking them would reveal the flag, but they are out of scope. Without safety prompts, GPT-6 Cyber stayed in scope 99.93% of the time, up from 94.49% for the older model. With the prompts, it hit 100%. Its reasoning notes show lines like “don’t explore out of scope credentials.” 81 Firefox Flaws OpenAI researchers gave Mozilla proof and test cases for 81 new bugs that Mozilla rates high severity. The model also showed that 30 known issues were worse than first reported. Mozilla’s advisory MFSA 2026-118 covers fixes in Firefox 159, released October 27. Many entries credit OpenAI Codex Security and OpenAI researchers. Most of the listed bugs are use-after-free memory errors in parts like layout, DOM, and JavaScript. Other AI models have hit Firefox too. Cyber Security News reported that Claude Mythos found 271 Firefox zero-days earlier this year. Brian Grinstead of Mozilla said Firefox was one of the most hardened codebases going into 2026, and the new bugs still turned up. 948 Linux Kernel Exploits OpenAI’s report, A thousand fewer paths to root , explains the Linux work. The pipeline picked 5,034 audit targets, about 7% of the kernel. It produced 2,308 candidate findings and reproduced 1,724 of them. It then built 948 working local privilege escalation exploits, which let a normal user become root. A GPT-5.6 Sol run in July found 166. The run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or about $1,279 per exploit. Past bounty prices would value the 948 exploits at $18.9 million to $66.3 million. OpenAI disclosed 304 critical findings with patches. Within 10 days, 61 had been fixed upstream and 43 had staged patches. Our earlier coverage details the 948 Linux kernel flaws . OpenAI says the agents used at least 10 new exploitation techniques. Outside kernel experts had not seen them before. One early run also showed why checks matter. Of 200 reported successes, 20 gained root through a different zero-day than the one assigned. OpenAI added an independent check for that. OpenAI added monitoring that checks whether actions match the user’s authorization. Daybreak Red API access requires IP allowlisting by default. The company also tracks stolen credentials and advises sandboxing and human review for risky work. For power plants and water systems, OpenAI added a Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure group and a $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders grant program. Dragos tested the model in a mock power plant. Chief AI Officer Rob T. Lee said it separated OT assets from IT noise and found two zero-days in engineering software that handles protective relay data. OpenAI’s advice is simple. Patch fast, rescan old code when models improve, and treat a low-privilege account on an unpatched system as close to root. It also stresses sandboxes like Firecracker and gVisor. The same group’s training environment report shows agents escaping microVMs during internal red-team tests. Teams can apply for Daybreak to request access. Dragos tested the model in a mock power plant. Chief AI Officer Rob T. Lee said it separated OT assets from IT noise and found two zero-days in engineering software that handles protective relay data.

OpenAI’s advice is simple. Patch fast, rescan old code when models improve, and treat a low-privilege account on an unpatched system as close to root. It also stresses sandboxes like Firecracker and gVisor. The same group’s training environment report shows agents escaping microVMs during internal red-team tests. items.title: Shopify Mandates IP Allowlisting for Public Apps to Prevent Unauthorized Admin API Access
items.summary: Shopify is making IP allowlisting mandatory for public apps that call its Admin API, adding a security check to limit the use of stolen access tokens. Developers must enable the control by November 20, 2026, at 11:59 PM ET. Apps using bulk operations face an earlier deadline of November 12 at the same time. The change turns a security feature introduced on October 27 into a requirement. Shopify will check where API requests come from, rather than relying on a valid token alone. This addresses the risk covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s cloud API security guide , where stolen credentials can give attackers access to cloud services. Once allowlisting is active, Shopify checks the source IP of GraphQL Admin API and REST Admin API requests using the app’s tokens. Requests from outside approved addresses or networks receive an HTTP 403 response. Shopify also rejects requests when it cannot confirm the source address. Apps that miss the November 20 deadline face removal from the Shopify App Store and blocked new installations. Existing installations can continue operating until April 1, 2027, when Admin API requests will fail. However, bulk queries and mutations face the earlier November 12 cutoff. Merchants will receive admin warnings from January 15. The policy targets token misuse, a risk illustrated by Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on the Internet Archive’s repeated breach through unrotated API tokens . Network restrictions add protection, but developers still need to secure their credentials. An attacker operating inside an approved network could remain within the permitted boundary. Shopify Mandates IP Allowlisting Shopify’s setup guide supports specific public IP addresses and address ranges for static infrastructure. Apps with changing addresses can approve hosting networks through autonomous system numbers, or ASNs. Developers can list up to 10 ASNs and narrow access to up to 10 countries. These network rules are broader than individual server addresses. Developers configure the control under Settings in the Dev Dashboard and test it against recent traffic before enabling enforcement. Shopify recommends checking whether legitimate requests would be blocked, then confirming an outside request fails. Apps must choose either IP addresses or networks, because saving one type replaces the other. Shopify’s official announcement lists November 12 in its detailed bulk-operation instructions, despite November 11 appearing in its summary. Separately, public apps must migrate to expiring offline tokens by January 1, 2027, adding time limits alongside network restrictions. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Microsoft Paint 0-Click Vulnerability Could Allow Hackers to Take Control of Windows PCs
items.summary: Microsoft’s Windows Paint vulnerability, CVE-2026-83844, could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code over a network without user interaction. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 8.1, placing it in the High severity category rather than Critical. However, confusion over the corrected Paint version has complicated patch checks for Windows administrators. The vulnerability stems from an out-of-bounds read, a memory error in which software reads beyond its intended boundary. Microsoft published the advisory on October 13, 2026. Its assessment lists a network attack vector, no required privileges, and high attack complexity, meaning successful exploitation depends on conditions that make an attack harder to carry out. Windows 0-Click Paint RCE Vulnerability The disclosure formed part of the October update cycle, covered in Cybersecurity News’ Microsoft October Patch Tuesday report . For administrators, the immediate concern is not simply whether an update exists, but whether the corrected application build has actually reached managed devices. Microsoft initially listed Paint version 11.2605.91.0 as the fixed release. Administrators reported that Microsoft Store continued offering 11.2605.81.0, even after update checks and Store cache resets. Microsoft’s advisory listed 11.2609.401.0 as the fix, suggesting the earlier version reference may have been incorrect. Microsoft has not confirmed that explanation. Update availability also appears inconsistent. Some administrators reported difficulty obtaining a corrected build, while one participant in the Reddit discussion said the update had become available through Microsoft Store. These individual reports do not establish a universal rollout status. Claims that availability depends on region also remain unverified. A crafted image could trigger the flaw, but Microsoft’s quoted guidance describes a crafted network packet sent to an affected service. The Hacker News discussion highlights the missing detail: neither the exposed service nor the complete attack path is identified. Suggestions involving Copilot or other components are speculation. Administrators should check the installed Paint version rather than trust an “up to date” message alone. Neowin recommends following Microsoft’s current advisory and considering temporary removal where Paint is unnecessary. Restricting untrusted images may reduce general exposure, but it is not a confirmed fix for this specific network attack path. Cybersecurity News’ separate PNG vulnerability coverage provides related context on image software security. Those flaws are separate from this Paint vulnerability. items.title: Groklem: an Android banker that rents Grok to read your texts
items.summary: A bank OTP lands on a phone somewhere in South Asia. Before the owner has even glanced at it, a background service has copied the message, scraped the last ten days of their texts to go with it, and shipped the bundle off with one instruction: find the money . Seconds later an answer comes back, not to the victim, but to a stranger on the other end of a socket: a tidy JSON summary of the victim’s bank accounts, their latest balance, and a guess at what’s in there right now. OTPs, card alerts, PIN resets, all sorted and labelled. The thief never read a single text himself.

items.title: Cardio-Driven Development
items.summary: I’ve been hard at work on some research projects and new roles that require me to learn topics I don’t know about (or at least have mostly forgotten about). For example, someone on my team came out with an interesting Linux kernel LPE and I felt like it was my responsibility to know everything I can about that exploit so I can help with disclosure or reporting. I run. I’m not fast. I don’t go particularly far. I just do it. If you’re a runner you might have thought about different running “zones.” Running fast is good for anaerobic work, while slower runs are better for aerobic. The test for whether you’re in Zone 2 is can you have a conversation while running or not.
